ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM PROPOSAL TO PERMIT WAGE INCREASES TO EQUAL INCREASES IN COST OF LIVING-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The rate of inflation, contrary to the assertion made in Vancouver yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), is increasing, not decreasing. We are now experiencing an average for the last three months of almost 11 per cent which is substantially higher than it was at the time when wage and price controls were imposed. In view of the fact that the government has indicated that wage and salary increases will be restricted to
six per cent which will mean a decline in the average Canadian family's standard of living of about S450 for 1978, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House calls upon the government to permit wage and salary increases within the framework of the controls program to at least match increases in the cost of living and thereby avoid any losses in our standard of living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the need to bring to light certain RCMP activities which are at least compromising, if not outright criminal, the reluctance of the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Fox) to co-operate with the inquiry commission which has been set up by the Quebec government, the doubts which are entertained regarding the objectivity of the McDonald Commission, which appears to be a duplicate of the Keable Commission, and because the whole thing is aimed apparently at covering up an ill advised authorization issued by the federal government, especially before, during and after the October 1970 crisis, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette):
That the House request the attorneys general and the justice ministers of all provinces to set up a fair and impartial joint inquiry commission to look into the criminal activities of the RCMP.

That this House instruct the Solicitor General to extend the terms of reference of the McDonald Commission in such a way as to allow witnesses not only to identify foreign powers operating within our national boundaries but to allow detailed exposures of any or all questionable practices by foreign interests operating in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. PROPOSED INCREASES IN COST OF AUTOMOBILES AND PETROLEUM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may 1 direct my supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Considering that there are two aspects of the cost of living
Oral Questions
in which the government does have a direct role to play and which are seriously affecting Canadians now-1 refer to the increases in the price of petroleum and cars-and considering the fact that General Motors, Chrysler and Ford all have profits substantially higher on the Canadian side of the border than on the U.S. side, according to a government report, would the government now take steps to ensure that the announced price increases which are coming in the automotive industry in January do not take place in Canada, and will he take steps to order the oil companies not to announce price increases in the petroleum sector which are also coming in January?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: PROPOSED INCREASES IN COST OF AUTOMOBILES AND PETROLEUM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the price of petroleum in this country has been kept, through enormous subsidies, below world prices, since the fall of 1973. Even the Leader of the NDP should understand that Canada cannot continue to subsidize forever its citizens with the taxpayers money and buy our oil in Canada at prices below world prices. This government, over a period of five years now, has brought these prices up slowly. They are moving towards world prices but have not yet reached them. Canadians will have to realize that the world prices for petroleum, the cost of investment in petroleum research and development in various parts of the world, these prices are at datum and we have to live with that. Once again the government has heavily subsidized in particular the five provinces of this country, and done it partly at the expense of the two western provinces, namely, Alberta and Saskatchewan. The NDP Premier of Saskatchewan has always complained that we have kept his prices too low; the NDP Leader in Ottawa is complaining that prices are too high. Mr. Speaker, this government has taken the view that a gradual phasing in of that price was the proper policy to adopt. But Canadians will have to face reality eventually, they will have to face the fact that those are the world prices for petroleum products.
There was also a second question. Perhaps 1 can deal with it next, Mr. Speaker.

Considering that the Premier of Saskatchewan, contrary to what the Prime Minister is alleging, has always maintained that any price increase should only take place if all the additional revenue were to go to the people of Canada instead of the oil companies, in flat contrast to the policies of this government, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would consider adopting the policy that has been implemented by the Premier of Saskatchewan for the whole of Canada.
Second, to come back to the question he did not answer that pertains directly to the increases in the consumer price index that were announced today, which pertains to automobiles that are owned by 80 per cent of the Canadian families who are paying anywhere up to $1,000 up more per car than Americans for vehicles produced in Canada, will he stop these companies from increasing the price of cars to Canadians this January?

subsubtopic: HMCS "ASSINIBOINE"
speechtext:
1.	What are the details concerning the unscheduled docking of HMCS Assiniboine which resulted in Shelburne Marine Ltd. of Shelburne, Nova Scotia getting a $110,062 contract?
2.	Were there other costs in connection with the unscheduled docking?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: HMCS "ASSINIBOINE"
speechtext:
1. In reply to a request for proposal, Saint John Shipbuilding and Drydock Co. Ltd., Saint John, N.B. offered a price of $172,754.58 for the known work, plus an allowance of $31,558 for estimated work arising, for a total estimated cost of $204,312.58. The Department of Supply and Services judged the price to be unacceptable and issued an invitation to tender to six companies. Only one bid was received, that of Saint John Shipbuilding and Drydock Co. Ltd. who tendered the same price as before. DSS did not consider this price to be acceptable for the work to be performed and led them to seek another source. As it happened, the delay in finalizing the price with Saint John Shipbuilding allowed another company to bid on the requirement since, in the interim, that company's docking facilities had been certified by DND as being able to dock the vessel concerned. Shelburne Marine Limited submitted a price of $110,061.68 for the known work plus an allowance of $30,540 for a like amount of work arising, as considered for Saint John Shipbuilding, for a total estimated cost of $140,601.68. The contract was therefore awarded to Shelburne and negotiations were terminated with Saint John Shipbuilding and Drydock Co. Ltd.
2. The total job including all work arising was completed at $146,914.36.

The House resumed, from Monday, December 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-ll, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the third time and do pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that this bill has had considerable examination; in fact, longer
December 13, 1977

than the government wanted. After two weeks in committee, I still have a few comments to add. I refer, first, to the statement that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) included in his economic and fiscal statement. At page 8, he said this:
First, I am cutting taxes for low and middle income taxpayers by $100.
He went on to say how that was to be done in order that there would be stimulation in the economy during the months of January and February. In committee, 1 raised the matter of these cuts with the minister or his parliamentary secretary, and asked whether they would really be effective. It had been drawn to my attention, through negotiations with the Minister of Finance and the ministers of finance for the provinces, that certain adjustments had been made in provincial tax rates, resulting in substantially increased provincial income tax rates.
A constituent of mine who is an income tax consultant worked out two examples, and 1 was able to show the minister that in fact a taxpayer would not be saving the amount of money through the tax cuts for which the Minister of Finance took credit. In some cases it would appear that with the increase in provincial tax rates, even though the federal rates had dropped, giving a saving in federal taxes, the additional increase in provincial taxes would actually result in a much smaller gain, or in some cases a loss. In other words, the taxpayer would end up paying more than he had previously.
Whilst we are at third reading stage of this bill I would like to refer to the life insurance provisions. We note the minister's own words at page 9 of his economic and fiscal statement. He said:
As a result of representations from members on all sides of the House, I will not be proceeding at this time with the measure for taxing the investment income realized by a policyholder on the death of the person insured.
It is nice to know, Mr. Speaker, that the government can be influenced by pressure. I wonder, at times, why they bring these things in in the first place. If they had thought them through initially, they would not have had the problem. During the committee stage, the minister introduced amendments which we were only too willing to receive on this side of the House. Interest on loans really is interest on loans, and following the time-honoured traditions of the Income Tax Act, money laid out to produce income should be deductible for income tax purposes.
We on this side of the House felt it was only fair that this should apply to anyone who has borrowed-it does not matter whether it is a policy loan-and some arguments were made that it is not really a loan when you borrow from an insurance company. I never could follow that argument. In any event, the government has finally realized that interest paid on that kind of loan should continue to be deductible. We welcome that move.
Now, this 3 per cent inventory allowance which may affect some individuals was, in the admission of the parliamentary secretary, an arbitrary figure. There does not seem to be any logical basis for having chosen 3 per cent. However, if one looks at the inflation rate, which surely must affect inventories as well as everything else, 3 per cent on inventories at a time when we have inflation of 8 per cent or 9 per cent is not going
Income Tax
to have the desired affect. It certainly will not solve the problem. The reason for having this provision in the first place was so that inflationary profits would not be taxed, and the effort that is being put forth by this 3 per cent allowance will not solve that problem.
I asked the minister, during the committee stage, why the last in, first out method had not been examined. I believe it was the parliamentary secretary who replied that it had been considered but was deemed to be more complicated. As an accountant, I wonder what could be fairer than trying to match current costs, that is, inventory purchases of today, with current revenues, that is, sales of today. It has always been a principle of good accounting practice that current costs should be matched against current revenues. However, the government do not seem to have gone that route and we are glad they are doing something in the area of relief on inventories, but I am not sure they have chosen the correct route.
I now turn respect to clause 16(2) of the bill. I should like to read part of it:
"15) That where a resident taxpayer so elects in his return of income for his 1977 or any subsequent taxation year, all his gains and losses for the year and all subsequent years from the disposition of shares (other than prescribed shares), bonds, debentures, notes or similar obligations issued by a Canadian Corporation shall be deemed to be capital gains and capital losses of the taxpayer, except where the taxpayer is a dealer or trader in securities-
There is a fundamental problem contained in this little section. I see it as the government digging a great big hole beside the taxpayer and inviting him to fall into it. I wish to refer to the committee hearings because the questions and answers are quite important here. The hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) asked whether it was going to affect individuals, entrepreneurs, explorers, and so on. He was talking about corporations. The parliamentary secretary said:
Mr. Chairman, this clause is written not only to assist individuals, but primarily venture investment corporations.
There we have it. It is designed to do both things, help venture corporations and assist individuals. There we have it in the words of the government. As reported at page 1739 of Hansard, I asked the parliamentary secretary the following question:
It it possible that subclause (2) could be used to the peril of an individual taxpayer who makes an election? I presume it is one he makes for life. A taxpayer might find himself in a position where he was in the business of trading in securities. If he had not made that election, he would have the right to declare his income and losses in the regular way. What about the man who might find himself in such a position?
The parliamentary secretary replied:
The hon. member is correct: it is a very difficult decision for an individual to make.
Already, under the law, an individual who is selling securities has the right, without making any election, to declare his gains and losses as capital gains and losses. Already, under the existing legislation, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay) has the right to decide that that individual is in the business of trading or dealing in securities and to say that the

December 13, 1977
Income Tax
income therefrom is not a capital gain but, rather, is income in the ordinary course of a taxpayer's business.
A taxpayer can already make that decision on a year by year basis. The government can already make the claim, which the taxpayer would have to disprove, that he is not entitled to make that declaration of that gain as a capital gain. What is the purpose of having a section like this, which is supposed to aid the individual, when obviously if you follow it through only harm will come to the taxpayer? If he makes the election, he has made it for life. That is quite clear. He can no longer go back and say that he wants to be in the business, if he should happen to be in the business; but the government has the option to come along later and say that in fact he was in the business.
I have another reference to the committee debate on this same point. I was quite surprised at the results. After lunch, on the same day, 1 asked the government about that election. 1 stated that I was concerned about this because it appeared to affect individual taxpayers as well as promoters and developers. I pointed out to the government as follows:
When an individual resident of Canada decides to make an election, he is bound by that election for the rest of his taxpaying years.
I explained to the government:
Subclause (2) (5) indicates that an election under subsection (4) does not apply to a disposition of a Canadian security by a taxpayer who, at the time the security is disposed of, is a trader or dealer in securities.
That is quite clear. The response by the parliamentary secretary was as follows:
Mr. Chairman, the answer to the question is yes. There is always a question of fact to be resolved in cases of this nature.
I asked:
Why did the government feel it was necessary or desirable to dig this large hole for taxpayers to fall into?
The parliamentary secretary replied:
I think that most individuals will know whether we are dealing in capital losses or gains, but the basic premise is to try to reduce uncertainty where there is doubt.
I submit the government has not done that at all. All they have done is put this terrible problem before the taxpayer who already has many problems arising out of the tax system. I do not want to take any more of the time of the House than necessary. I will conclude by urging the government to look at these situations before putting them into the proposed legislation which, with the action of closure that was imposed by the government on the House, means that these problems are not solved.
Since 1970, this government has been promising us simplicity and equity in our income tax law. That was the reason given for the tax reform legislation put before this parliament. It is obvious to anyone who has been studying Bill C-l 1, and to all taxpayers in Canada who in the next four months will be wrestling with their income tax returns, that we have neither simplicity nor equity in the tax system in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wish to thank the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke)

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even if, like the government and my colleagues, I would like to end the study of Bill C-ll, I will want to participate in the debate on third reading to make some positive criticism on this piece of legislation.
It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that a bill with 116 clauses could not be studied in one scoop. As far as we are concerned, the government has no reason to complain about filibuster because we have limited our speeches as much as possible. However, it is our duty to express our views by defending the interests of our constituents. First of all, I appreciate that the employment expense allowance has been increased from $150 to $250 starting from 1977. However, it is not sufficient. The government should consider that workers who must travel a long way to and from work have increasing expenses because of inflation. Corporations have the privilege of entering the travelling expenses of their employees as deductible expenses but it is not the same for an individual. Therefore, my colleague the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) put forward an amendment to clause 4 of the bill proposing to raise the deductible amount to $400. The amendment was turned down by the government majority.
I therefore urge once again the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to accept an amendment increasing the deduction to at least $400. I think that would be fair to workers who must necessarily incur expenses each day to go to work. The government is now convinced that it is urgent to boost personal income to stimulate the national economy and for that purpose, it is granting a $100 income tax reduction. Taking into account the fact that individuals get only 40 per cent of the national income comparatively to 60 per cent for corporations, while individuals pay 60 per cent of taxes and corporations only 40 per cent, it is urgent that the government seriously consider a readjustment of tax distribution to make it more reasonable.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-ll provides an economic incentive for the Maritimes and the Gaspe Peninsula through tax benefits. However, I wonder why the Minister of Finance has excluded from those benefits the south shore area between Levis and Riviere-du-Loup. I even wrote to the Minister of Finance in that connection to ask him to introduce an amendment to clause 60(10) to include in Bill C-ll the Bellechasse constituency which is part of the south shore. Unfortunately, the amendment was not introduced, so the industrialists and private concerns of this area will be deprived of those benefits since, even if they are limited it is with those scraps that an area can develop and provide employment for workers. Mont-magny is a town of 13,000 inhabitants founded many years
December 13, 1977

ago with many activities, but it has remained stagnant for some years, not because it has been represented in the Canadian Parliament by this speaker, this is not important, because what is important is to use local benefits, in Montmagny as elsewhere, to urge the industries to grow and other individuals to set up business to allow a normal development.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to give an example. There are three textile industries in Montmagny and it is because of the tenacity of the administrators of those industries that they have managed to survive, even if the number of jobs has come down. I would like to give certified figures which do show that imports have had harmful effects on the development of the industries located in Montmagny. For example, take the case of Bermatex Inc., an industry which was set up a few years ago and provided many jobs. That little business provided a livelihood for 60 people three years ago. Today, as I am speaking to you, there are about 37. This means that there has been a substantial drop. Yet in spite of all the inconveniences, the fact is that the price for a pound of texturized polyester thread, which was $1.85 three years ago, is now $1.30. That is why I say the administrators of those companies are making unbelievable efforts to try and continue to operate and maintain a reasonable level of employment.
In 1973, only four years ago, Consolidated Textiles provided employment for 187 people and there are now 123. And in 1975 the company had to make a choice: close its doors or continue to operate without profit. It chose the second option and continued to operate with very modest or no profits. So, for the last two years, the Montmagny plant has been operating at near capacity but it must sell its product at cost prices. It is also producing inventory but it is starting to get very high. These are details I obtained from the administrators themselves. They cannot do any long-term planning now because of market uncertainty and they could very well be closing down in a month or two. They have been waiting for an economic recovery for two years and they are beginning to get discouraged.
I also met the owners of Dionne Spinning. They told me of their concerns about the market because of massive imports which are not curbed fast enough and if we continue in that direction, we are soon going to see another gearing down in the operations of those textile companies. Unemployment is going to go up and we are going to find ourselves in an excessively serious situation.
To administer is to foresee; that is why I draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) those very important matters. I should also like to give some figures to prove what I just said about the textile industry. In 1976, retail sales in the clothing industry amounted to $5.5 billion in Canada. The textile and clothing industries give employment to 200,000 Canadian workers. Those jobs represent one in twelve in the Canadian manufacturing industry. In Quebec, those jobs represent one in four jobs. In other words, they have considerable importance, representing as they do 70 per cent of all manufactures and 65 per cent of all jobs in the Quebec clothing industry.
Income Tax
But Quebec city is in Canada, and I hope that it will continue to be, even though some people occasionally try to spread the rumor that the Social Credit Party of Canada is a separatist party. For my part, I do not believe this. I know what I am. I am in favor of a true Canada, but I want all the regions of Canada to be treated fairly. This is what a central government should do. It should ensure fair distribution and give equal opportunities to all areas of the country, and when one area has certain economic difficulties, it is the responsibility of the federal government to take action and try to give special treatment to this area so that its residents can have a standard of living that is at least equal to that of other Canadians. Mr. Speaker, more than ever today, we must find immediate answers to help the remote areas of Canada since the businesses, companies and industries which operate in these areas do not have the same advantages as those in large centres. This is why there must be special programs to enable those businesses to operate at a production cost comparable to that of plants established in major centres so that they will receive orders for their products, sell those products, stay in business and give employment to the workers of the area who will then be able to pay the same taxes as other Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, many of these businesses are in small communities which depend on them for their survival. These industries are established in high unemployment areas. I would like to quote a few figures to show that the Textile and Clothing Import Control Board did not do its job. From 1970 to 1976, imports increased by 145 per cent. Imports from Taiwan increased from 973,000 units in 1961 to 80 million units in 1976. Imports from the Republic of Korea increased by 1,000 per cent between 1970 and 1976. Mr. Speaker, clothing imports per capita in Canada are among the largest in the world. But the percentage of total Canadian imports subject to limitations are among the smallest. In the United States for instance 71 per cent of imports are restricted and Americans spend $11.50 per capita on imported clothing.
What is then the situation in Canada? Only 7 per cent of imports are restricted while Canadians spend $19.50 per capita on imported clothing. That is why I say that while the 1970 Canadian textile policy may have helped the Canadian industry, it certainly did not succeed in curbing the steady rise of imports. Even the new quotas imposed on November 29, 1977 did not bring much change. Again, we must acknowledge the failure of this policy since it has not led to significant improvement.
Mr. Speaker, I shall quote another example: Old quotas allowed the importation of 726,000 sweaters from the Republic of Korea. New quotas allowed the importation of 704,000 sweaters over the same period of time, that is only a 3 per cent reduction, which is not enough. Now, as far as the market is concerned, in 1971, the domestic market share was 73 per cent and the importation market share, 27 per cent. In 1976, importations accounted for 45 per cent of the Canadian market while in 1975, they were almost stable. One year later, they had increased by 10 per cent while the domestic market

December 13, 1977
Income Tax
fell from 73 per cent in 1971 down to 55 per cent of the market.
Mr. Speaker, 1 quoted those figures to demonstrate that we should apply our control policy more strictly to help our industries face these difficult times. It may seem a good idea to import sweaters for $3.00 when it cost $3.25 to manufacture them in Canada. There is a 25 cent difference, but if our youth is unemployed, do you think we are better off buying those sweaters for $3.00 when with 25 cents more we could buy them here and provide jobs for our people? If we keep buying foreign goods because it is cheaper, while Canadian workers are unemployed or on welfare, we can be sure of one thing: People who are working will be taxed and overtaxed and one day or the other, they will get discouraged and refuse to support all those who are doing nothing while they have to work around the clock.
Mr. Speaker, here again it is the duty of the government to use every possible means to give all able bodied men and women an opportunity to contribute to the gross national product and work in our country even if it means spending a few dollars more on consumer goods.
We just voted before the weekend special estimates under which the government is empowered to borrow an amount of $9 billion for administrative purposes in Canada. And certainly, what with the borrowing policy of this government and the public sector financing needs, a major part of those $9 billion will go in debt servicing. Further opportunities for profit will be given to those who are in control, who have the monopoly over the process of monetizing the nation's credit. This is the most outraging aspect of the management of public affairs. In this country, we are forced to crawl before those who control the nation's credit in order to produce things, to ensure the services needed by the people.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put forward a proposal to change the situation. We are told sometimes that we never make any positive suggestions, well I just made one, and I would like to make another. Namely that the federal tax on building materials be lowered. That tax significantly increases building costs because it adds to the cost of materials and to the provincial tax. Tax over tax, this is senseless. What would happen if we abolished the tax on building materials? I am just about convinced that if we lowered the interest rates and the tax on building materials, then we would see the realization of many projects dear to the hearts of Canadians. Construction would gain momentum. Masons would be at work and so would bricklayers. For houses and buildings made out of bricks, bricklayers would be necessary, carpenters and day labourers would be at work, as would roofers, electricians, plumbers, merchants and those people who engage in transportation. Just imagine the impact of two such proposals as lowering interest rates and lowering or repealing the tax on building materials. Just imagine how many workers could be given employment, not to mention office personnel who would have more work to perform because there would be more invoicing, more collections, more phone calls, more communications-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Except for the economists!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Except for the economists, that's right, for they work only when everything goes well. They give recipes when everything is working well. But when everything goes sour, they just withdraw by saying: Find your own solution to your problems! This is just about what they are doing with this present government which has to tackle with major problems and even if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said today that economists have told him that only Japan is going to be in a better economic position than Canada next year you may find another economist who is going to say just the opposite in January. They are not numerous yet they cannot seem to agree among themselves.
It is quite a problem today to trust economists. Why? Not because they do not know anything. Of course not. Indeed they know a lot of things, but they want to administer in 1977-78 with old formulas dating back to 25, 30 or 40 years ago, when there were fewer innovations, less progress than today, when it took more manpower to accomplish all sorts of things. They want to administer in the same way, though it is impossible. We are not going to scrap our tractors, do away with innovations for the sheer pleasure of saying that we are going to put men to work. If this is the objective, if such are the formulas chosen by our economists . . . Incidently during the weekend I saw a power shovel in my riding and it did a very good job, there was only one operator, but if we are to do away with progress and innovations in order to be in tune with the spirit of the day, namely to hire 100 workers with small shovels that are three feet long, small round shovels, and if there are still people without jobs, to hire them to work with teaspoons, that does not make any sense. What is being suggested to us looks very much like that.
Mr. Speaker, there is also an electrical panel box manufacture in Montmagny; its operations were a real success and helped, I believe, 90 workers; today it has barely 30 employees and the business is having a hard time of it. Why? Because construction is at a standstill, the plant gets no orders and therefore manufacturing has stopped. In other words, the situation is really serious on the south shore. That is why I should have liked the Minister of Finance to take that into account in clause 60(10) of Bill C-ll. I am asking him once again to consider seriously the possibility of amending that clause.
I should also like to speak for a few minutes of a problem concerning the Canadian economy. Unfortunately, as early as a month or even five weeks ago, too many of our dairy producers exhausted their quotas until next April. To those of them who send their milk to the processing plant, a penalty will apply, namely a fine of $7 per hundredweight. It is better for them not to send it. If they do not deliver it, the milk will have to be thrown away and this does not pay much. These people have obligations to meet, they must live and if we do not find a way out pretty soon, many of them will go bankrupt. The Canadian tax structure is detrimental to economic development. It discourages investment and entrepreneurship. It encourages the flight of accumulated capital from this country.
I do not think anybody has any idea of how many entrepreneurs in this country have created vehicles outside this country by which to avoid the capital gains tax, income tax and other taxes which this government has imposed in a non-competitive way. The government wants money in a hurry.

The agricultural industry needs a change in the tax structure and in the tariff structure. The policies of the Department of Agriculture need changing. Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) has done, I would like to say a few words about one issue which is not dealt with by this bill; that is the issue of agriculture and farming. The time has come when we should examine our taxation system as it affects farmers. One need only look at the income figures which were released yesterday to determine why that must be done.
At the Outlook Conference here in Ottawa yesterday, it was announced by the Department of Agriculture and by Statistics Canada that the net income of farmers will fall 11 per cent in 1977 over 1976. To put that in perspective, the net income of farmers in 1976 fell by some 20 per cent over 1975. The forecast for next year, as reported in all the newspapers today, is that net income for farmers is likely to fall by another 6.1 per cent in 1978. When a situation like that exists, I do not think any member of this House has to be convinced that many farmers across the country are in dire financial straits at the present time. Their income has fallen for two years in a row, and will fall again in 1978.
What should be done about this situation? There are many things which could be done. As other hon. members have done I have in the past made many speeches about farming, food and agriculture in general, but I want to point out one or two things today about which I think all of us should be aware.
As we know from the statistics released yesterday, farm income has fallen but the consumer price index in respect of the price of food is rising. Just this morning we received statistics which show that the price of food went up by 13.9 per cent between November of last year and November of this year. The price of food consumed in the home went up by 15.9 per cent. When farm income is going down at such drastic rates as 20 per cent last year, 11 per cent this year, and another 6 per cent next year, why is it that the price of food is going up by 12 per cent, 13 per cent and 14 per cent?
The time has come when the government should take a serious look at the middlemen in the food chain and find out why the price of food is going up so sharply while farm income is going down. Our consumers need protection, but the government should also be doing a number of things to protect farmers. Some of these things can be done through our tax system. As the previous speaker said, a number of things can
Income Tax
be done now to help farmers. The price of wheat has gone down sharply in the last two years; it has dropped radically. The price of wheat is so low that when a farmer produces wheat, he barely meets the cost of production. It costs him almost as much to produce wheat as he is getting for it when he sells it to the grain elevator for sale overseas or for domestic use.
I think the government in general, and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board in particular, should be moving to ensure that farmers now receive a pay-out from the western grain stabilization fund. That pay-out should be made now, not when an election is announced, which will probably be next March, April or May. The government now has figures on farm income and that income is away down. Farmers deserve a pay-out and I suggest that one should be made now.
As we conclude this debate on taxation and income and how we distribute wealth and income, we should take a few moments to consider the farm income statistics to which I have been referring. We should study the net income of farmers, that is, farm income after costs, depreciation, and so forth. In 1977, net farm income will be $3.3 billion. In 1978, the figure is expected to go down to $3.1 billion. That will be a drop of 6.1 per cent.
At the same time, farm costs are going up and will go up very rapidly. In 1976, farm costs amounted to $7.3 billion, according to federal government statistics revealed at the Outlook Conference yesterday. In 1977, farm costs will rise to $7.8 billion. In 1978, they are expected to rise still further, to $8.3 billion. Hon. members can see that despite the fact that farm income is going down rapidly, farm costs are going up. Thus, the farmer is caught in the cost-price squeeze, the classic phrase we have used on the prairies for so long. The amounts farmers receive for their commodities are going down or staying at the same level, but the price farmers have to pay to produce a bushel of wheat, to raise a steer or a hog, or to produce vegetables or fruit, is going up. How long can this situation continue before farmers are forced off their land? At a time like this the government should be examining farm income and proposing changes which we could pass in this House in order to alleviate the problem.
I want to discuss farm costs for a moment. Many things could be done about high farm costs. I have in my hand a document which was produced for the Outlook Conference, entitled "Farm Inputs". It is dated December, 1977, and was produced by Agriculture Canada. This document states the following:
Although 1977 was a poor year for farm machinery sales compared with 1976, next year looks worse. Manufacturers and distributors of machinery in Canada will face a large decrease in sales volume; their inventories will continue to grow; their margins and profits will fall; and farmers will have little relief from price increases.
Despite the fact that farmers are buying less and less farm machinery-and making fewer repairs because their income has fallen-and despite the fact that the inventory of farm machinery in this country is very high the price of farm machinery remains very high. There is no law of supply and

December 13, 1977

demand when it comes to farm machinery. Since farmers cannot afford to buy much machinery, one would think the price would be lower; but it has not yet fallen. The government has not told the farm machinery to lower their prices. Of course, it is not just farmers who are suffering, because many people in the farm machinery industry were laid off during the past year. Even in my riding, which does not have much manufacturing, over 100 people have been or will be laid off by the end of the year. 1 refer to the farm machinery industry in Yorkton. Companies such as Massey-Ferguson, Co-op Implements, Versatile and International Harvester have been laying off people because of the drop in farm income and the fact that there is no additional tax relief for farmers.
If any other sector of the economy had suffered the drop in real income that farmers have in the last two years, tax relief would be provided. If corporation profits had decreased by 20 per cent last year and 11 per cent this year, I am sure there would be more tax relief to corporations than is available to farmers. No relief is provided in the bill before us.
The government has conducted many studies of this situation. In the 1960s, a one-man commission under Clarence L. Barber was appointed to study the farm machinery industry. An interim report was produced in 1969 and the final report in 1971. However, I understand the government has put this report on the shelf and is no longer considering its recommendations. Apparently it has no intention of implementing any more of the suggestions made in the report. Its report painted quite a dark picture which endorses the view of the Outlook Conference as expressed in the paragraph I read into the record a few moments ago.
I should like to quote from the Journal of Economics of May, 1972, which I think summarizes the findings of the report very well. A review of the report of the Royal Commission on Farm Machinery, at page 316, reads in part as follows:
The picture of the industry that is drawn in the report is a classic picture of oligopoly: high concentration of output and sales, a history of mergers, entry obstructed by economies of scale in manufacturing and high investment in distribution, restraints on price competition among the leading firms and a gradual decline in their market share, significant price discrimination protected by monopolistic practices, emphasis on non-price competition, failure to exploit fully the economies of scale and to achieve maximum technical efficiency. All these features are discussed and, to some extent, analysed.
The report of the Barber commission gives many examples of an oligopoly in the industry, but the government has taken no action despite the recommendations. I suggest that in a sector where income has dropped so drastically in the last couple of years, the bill should make some effort to improve the position of the farmers.
A number of things other than favourable tax provisions could be done to help the agricultural industry in Canada. I should like to mention just one, tariffs. On average, the agricultural tariff in Canada is less than one-half of 1 per cent. This is one of the reasons we are not self-sufficient in food. When I was in the Niagara peninsula last May, I spoke to fruit and vegetable growers and found that we were no longer

self-sufficient in many areas where we used to be, because of lack of tariffs to prevent the dumping of certain fruits and vegetables by other countries.
Producers in that area would like a seasonal tariff so there would be some protection for their crops when they reach the market. It is strange that in this country some industries- many located in southern Ontario-have huge tariff walls. For many manufacturing industries the tariff is set at around 20 per cent, but the average farm tariff is less than one-half of 1 per cent.
Our farmers are very productive, Mr. Speaker. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) complains about productivity, I do not think he is referring to the farmers.

As the Science Council of Canada has warned, it is possible that by the year 2000 we will not be self-sufficient in food but will be a net importer, despite our vast acreage and all our technology. Mr. Speaker, because other members wish to speak before five o'clock, I should like to end by saying to the government, again, that the next time a tax bill is brought before the House it should include measures to protect our food producers. 1 would remind the House that last year farmers suffered a drop in net income of 20 per cent, and may suffer a drop of 11 per cent this year-that is, 11 per cent on the 20 per cent-which is a sharp drop over two years. The experts say that next year it will drop by about 6.1 per cent.
The time has come for better planning in the food and agricultural sector of the economy. This could be achieved through progressive tax changes which would help small and middle-sized farmers stay on the land. They would produce more food, make this a better country for all and, hopefully, in an area in which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) is so interested, make a greater contribution to help feed the world.

ing on the bill he referred to last October 20. What an utter disgrace we have here.

I believe that all of us-as consumers, workers, businessmen, or politicians- recognize that the economy cannot be expected to continue to deliver the increases in real incomes that we enjoyed in the relatively easy times of the 1960s and early 1970s.
First as a consumer, second as a businessman, third as a worker, and finally as a politician, I want to dissociate myself from that pessimistic attitude the Minister of Finance took in Vancouver. 1 dissociate the Conservative caucus from the suggestion that we cannot regain the real growth potential that should be ours in Canada. I know there are those who believe parliament is becoming-the Prime Minister likes to express this view-increasingly irrelevant, that its institutions are inadequate to cope with today's problems and its committee system, in particular, is little more than a ritualistic exercise which has a marginal impact, say, on unemployment, inflation or the other economic woes to which I have referred. Cast your mind back to a week ago last Friday when the Minister of Finance made one of the few, short appearances he has consented to make before the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. At that time, Mr. Speaker, we were pressing the minister to tell us more about how he was going to relieve the $11 billion end product, manufactured goods, trade deficit we are now experiencing. We asked how he was the going to relieve $11 billion deficit in order to achieve approximately 800,000 jobs that such a deficit means? Lo and behold, what did the Minister of Finance tell us? He told us it was a question of terminology; in fact, it was somehow just a question of definition. For example, wheat really was an end product; if you took wheat and included it in manufactured goods, our over-all picture would look a lot better.

It is important we explore briefly the impact of the Minister of Finance's startling observation that wheat, rather than being a resource commodity, is somehow a manufactured commodity and we are, accordingly, doing much better than we thought. If I might, to specifically quote the Minister of Finance, he said:
How much further can one go in the exportation process? After all, we could scarcely be expected to bake bread for the Russians.
We can ship them wheat if we define it as a manufactured article and then our manufacturing imbalance will look much better because, after all, in the mind of the Minister of Finance wheat is manufactured. I admit that the depth of this idea absorbed us for a time at committee. In the first place, it means-as I said-that our trade imbalance in manufactured goods this year will not really top $11 billion. If we accept the terminology of the Minister of Finance, all we have to do is accept wheat as a finished product. With a simple change of definition, the minister managed to arrest our alarming mounting deficit in manufactured trade-a problem, frankly, that absolutely defeated former ministers of finance to resolve.
That is only the beginning of the impact of this revolutionary way of approaching trade. If the minister's definition of finished products should catch on in the world, then Brazil, Colombia, the Ivory Coast, Angola, Uganda, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Honduras could become important new exporters of finished products. The first five nations I mentioned are the leading exporters of coffee and, to paraphrase the minister, we can scarcely export them to brew it for us. The last three countries are the leading exporters of bananas, and you can imagine their surprise when they discover that they have been exporting manufactured, end products all these years. What more perfect commodity could there be than a banana? It even comes in its own packaging and, as my colleague said, manufactured by God. The banana fits all the criteria of the minister's new definition: it is finished to such degree that there is nothing left to do but export it.
If the minister's definition catches on, then Thailand and Pakistan are important new exporters of finished end products. These nations are the second and third largest exporters of rice, and we can scarcely expect them to make rice pudding for us. This should make the Thais and the Pakistanis very happy, as they have been labouring under the mistaken impression all these years that they were not exporters of manufactured or finished goods.
The new system, however, will not make everyone happy. If the minister is right, then Japan will become a major importer of finished goods, in that she imports about $1.1 billion worth of wheat each year. This is only part of the picture. Poor Japan also imports massive amounts of tea, rice, coffee and other finished products. I suppose it will be only a matter of time before Japan is knocking on the World Bank's door for a loan to help them cope with their staggering deficit in finished products.

What of our neighbours to the south? The minister told the committee that it is not only wheat or barley or the other grains that should be considered as finished goods, but newsprint as well. Imagine the Americans' surprise when they discover that they have squandered away their strong position in the trade of manufactured products by becoming the largest importers of newsprint. Maybe now it is a little more understandable why we have been so generous in giving them export assistance. With such a large debt accruing to us in finished products such as newsprint, the least we can do is build a few steel mills in Texas and New Jersey.
What an amazing breakthrough the minister has charted for the world! With one simple definition he has turned the world upside down. Yesterday's underdeveloped nations are now our major developed ones, and the developed country of yesterday is today's have-not country. We in Canada should be grateful to have such a genius to set the world straight.

Others may have their Adam Smiths, their Keyneses, Friedmans and Galbraiths; but perhaps the greatest of them all is our current Minister of Finance who continues to dazzle us with reasoning akin to the man who wanted to change the name of Toronto to Miami in order to bring a warmer climate to Canada. We need not worry about our staggering deficit in manufactured items or the hundreds of thousands of lost Canadian jobs which that deficit implies. We need not concern ourselves with these things, the minister tells us, because he can simply redefine our trade statistics to make us look good. Calling wheat a finished product would not create any more jobs than before-but no matter, the minister could always redefine unemployment, too, and that problem would be no more.
In the meantime, of course, the minister is returning us, month by month, into a colonial state. We can export all the food and natural resources we want, and import all the manufactured items we want and the minister will set the books right by declaring wheat and newsprint as finished products. I recommend that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tell that to the jobless who are looking for work, especially in the manufacturing field.
It is too bad the minister was not around when the Fathers of Confederation tried to chart a course for Canada that would make it a manufacturing state. The minister could have saved them much worry by telling them that we were already a manufacturing country, that we have our own wheat and, "After all, you can't expect us to bake bread for the Russians." The minister could have told Macdonald that the entire concept of wanting Canada to manufacture goods for export was unnecessary, in that we were already a great exporter of
December 13, 1977

finished products. Such an approach to foreign trade might have changed the entire history of this country.
Looking ahead, with an election coming up, we fancy that the Liberals will want to campaign on this revolutionary concept in trade, and we envisage some 280 Liberal candidates pointing out that the government's policies of the last ten years have put Canada up there with the big ones, with Angola and Costa Rica, with Uganda and the Ivory Coast. No more will people laugh at banana republics. Thanks to the minister's new concept, such countries will become major exporters of finished goods and Canada will be right there with them.
I mention these things because we have in Bill C-ll the epitome, in legislative form, of the government's complacent, stagnant attitude with respect to the economic needs of the country. During second reading and committee of the whole stage we on this side advanced various proposals which we felt would improve the bill. Unfortunately, amendments were forthcoming in only two or three instances.
Bill C-56 proposed the taxation of life insurance policies- the first time such a thing had been done not only in Canada but anywhere else in the world. I am pleased that largely as a result of pressure from this side of the House the government has since backed down and Bill C-ll has been amended further to make taxation of life insurance policies less offensive to those who demanded that their life insurance policies should not be taxed by this government or by any government.
I am pleased, too, that the government has acceded to our request to give the benefit of an income tax cut to all Canadians, especially to those with modest means. But I am disappointed that the increase is so small and that by the use of closure the minister was able to cut off debate concerning the adequacy of the $100 reduction proposed in the bill. If we had been allowed to debate that clause, we would have asked the Minister of Finance if $2 a week was all Canadians needed by way of a tax cut. But we were not given that opportunity.
Many reasons have been advanced to explain the introduction of closure with respect to Bill C-ll, but when all attempts at rationalization have been forgotten, one reason will remain: the Minister of Finance is over his head when dealing with such legislation as this and the longer this subject is debated, the more his lack of depth is demonstrated on the floor of the House. That is why closure was introduced.
During the debate in committee of the whole we were able to bring out certain facts concerning the impact of the capital gains tax. We showed that to the extent the department was taxing capital gains without indexing for inflation, its actions were confiscatory. Hopefully, in a future budget the minister may see the need to put a stop to non-indexed taxation of capital gains. In short, nothing has contributed more to the inflation experience in land prices than the capital gains tax the government imposed a few years ago.
My time is limited, Mr. Speaker. I just wanted to touch on some of the highlights of the debate and draw attention to certain areas in which we feel the bill is particularly deficient.
Income Tax
I wanted to explain why we felt there was no alternative before us but to vote against Bill C-ll. We had hoped the legislation could be improved during the committee stage. We had hoped to persuade the government to increase the employee expenses allowance to $400 rather than the $250 presently proposed. But members opposite used the sheer weight of their majority to deny this to Canadian workers.
We had hoped to get the minister to agree to amend the Income Tax Act so as to remove the social insurance number provision; we do not feel these numbers should play any part in legislation such as this. These social insurance numbers have no place in our income tax system. I am sorry the Minister of Finance did not accede to our request for their removal. I am sorry he cut off debate to prevent members on this side asking him questions as to why he is seeking a further $9 billion in borrowing authority under clause 116 of the measure we are being asked to vote on this afternoon. These are the things which in future weeks the minister will, no doubt, regret having done.
The fact is, there is nothing in Bill C-ll which will in the coming months relieve the unemployment situation, the inflation we are now experiencing, the lack of real growth in the economy, or the tremendous deficit the government is living with. In short, no person who has any sense of responsibility should be prepared to sit in this chamber and vote support for a government which has shown that it is totally inadequate to cope with all these economic problems. In voting against Bill C-ll we are, in effect, voting against the government's economic record, and I call upon all members of the House to do likewise.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-8, to amend the Canada Labour Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
December 13, 1977

He said: I am sure hon. members have had a chance to look at Bill C-8, certainly in terms of its general purpose and its immediate objectives of improving the industrial relations system and Canada's competitive position.
Many of the provisions of the bill should be seen against the background of what my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), said a few weeks ago in his introduction of some other economic measures to stimulate the economy. Hon. members will recall that at that time he outlined the seriousness of our economic situation. He mentioned the rate of inflation was decreasing, yet it still had a long way to go to enhance our economic performance and position.
In addition he indicated that our output for this year and some of the projections for next year are not as great as we had hoped or as we earlier expected. But despite the fact that we can take some satisfaction in knowing that 250,000 more jobs have been created this year, there are still more Canadians requiring jobs.
The number of Canadians who need jobs is rising faster than the additional job creation that has occurred.
The Minister of Finance also indicated that although we have a favourable balance of payments on the trade side-a surplus of $2 billion-this is more than offset by a deficit in our tourist trade, interest payments, dividends, and so on. With that realistic analysis of the economic situation it becomes more imperative than ever that we improve our labour management relations system in Canada. The fundamental rationale behind the bill is to foster a greater degree of co-operation between management, labour and government in order to tackle some of these problems.
One of the underlying hopes in the bill is that it will foster a greater trend toward participation in various types of consulting mechanisms between government, labour, and management. Before dealing at any great length with those hopes, and just talking about the bill in specific terms, it would be useful if members looked at it in terms of it being divided essentially into three parts.
Which headings embody the objectives of the bill? We are talking first about justice in the work place. Under that meritorious objective, we should put in context the amendments in the bill to Parts III and IV of the Canada Labour Code.
Parts III and IV largely deal with upgrading the labour standards and enhancing the standards, particularly of the unorganized worker, and further, upgrading the safety and occupational health standards of the unorganized worker.
We should realize right away that the immediate impact of these provisions will be on the 550,000 workers under federal jurisdiction. They are primarily in the following areas in the federal sector: railroads, airlines, banking, trucking, broadcasting, grainhandling, communications, and the ports. About half of those 550,000 are unorganized.
Canada Labour Code
It is our hope that Parts III and IV will give at least to the unorganized workers some of the minimum standards which have been won by the organized workers and which are now embodied in their collective agreements. We are not alleging for one moment that they match the standards set out in collective agreements, but we provide here a minimum standard.
With that background, I would like to identify quickly what we propose in terms of Parts III and IV of the Labour Code.
The amendments seek primarily to provide workers with increased job protection. For example, the amendments will extend all benefits of the Code, except those related to hours of work, to managerial and professional employees, providing them for the first time with statutory rights with respect to such basic standards as vacations with pay and general holidays.
Dealing with pregnancy, this will not be acceptable as a cause for lay-off or dismissal. Under the present standard, employers may dismiss an employee with less than 12 months' service solely because of pregnancy. This will be corrected by this amendment.
Additional Part III amendments will provide paid leave to qualified employees when a member of their family dies. They will provide employees with basic job protection during periods of sickness. They will extend protection against unjust firing, with the right to appeal. They will require employers to pay all wages due to employees on a regular and timely basis. The bill also seeks to increase to nine the number of statutory holidays by the addition of Boxing Day.
Dealing with the highlights of the amendments to Part IV, and still dealing with the objective of justice in the work place, the proposals enhance the already comprehensive measures for protecting the safety and health of workers. Specifically, the amendments will first enable the establishment of employer-employee safety and health committees at the worker level which will identify and ensure the correction of work hazards.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
They will also provide employees with a voice in matters related to safe working conditions.
A further proposal would give workers the right to withdraw, without loss of pay, from work situations which they consider pose imminent personal danger. This would be a mechanism by which individual employees could exercise a responsibility, and a right, to remove themselves from work situations which, in their judgment, threatened injury to themselves.
There are provisions to ensure that they are protected against sanctions being unjustly applied to them in the exercise of that particular right.
Those are the proposals which deal with the main highlights in terms of justice in the work place.

December 13, 1977
Canada Labour Code
The second main objective of the bill is to accomplish improvements in the structures of collective bargaining. This is to be done through amendments to Part V of the Code. These amendments deal mainly with improving the system and the procedures of our industrial relations system.
At this juncture I would stress that despite the stresses and strains to which it has been subjected, our collective bargaining process continues to be viable. It will continue to receive the full support of this government.
As it now stands, Part V does allow certain adversarial tensions to remain unchecked, to accumulate, and therefore sometimes to disrupt the system.
The proposals now before the House have the following objectives: to reinforce the collective bargaining system in order to reduce some of the tensions between labour and management; to improve the grievance arbitration system, as another means of reducing tensions; to reduce tensions arising out of the relationships between the individual employee-union member and his union by increasing the protection of the rights of the individual; to reduce the impact upon the public of the adversarial nature of the system by affording greater protection of the public interest; and to reduce unnecessary delays and procedures in the administration of the collective bargaining process.
More specifically the amendments would require unions to furnish members with financial statements; would give the Canada Labour Relations Board more discretion to order representation votes and related run-off votes; would require that unions fairly represent members of the bargaining unit; would ensure fair and objective referral procedures by union hiring halls; and would authorize the CLRB to establish the terms of a first agreement, on referral from the minister.
These amendments would also provide interim certification so that certifications are not held up where there are very serious contentious points requiring further deliberation by the board but which do not in essence affect the union's right to certification. The board could avoid delays by granting interim certification.
Those are the proposals which deal with improving the process and, I emphasize, the process of the collective bargaining system.
As far as improving the structures within which the system operates, the bill provides for only some of the proposals in the 14-point program. They are largely the proposals that you can legislate. Many of the other proposals to improve the structure really do not lend themselves to legislative treatment. They are dependent upon a consultative process that would involve labour, management, and government. Because they depend for their success on consensus, they do not lend themselves to legislative treatment. I might identify a few of these so that these amendments can be seen in the over-all context of what the government hopes to achieve.

First, in terms of structure, we are hoping to set up a collective bargaining information centre. It would be a centre under the aegis of labour, management, and government as equal partners. They would be responsible for the operations of the centre. We then hope the centre would bring out data of an economic nature dealing with collective agreements, industry by industry, in a form which would be of immediate use to the parties at the bargaining table. The data would not be suspect in terms of having a bias as is so much of the data upon which our system relies. We have many agencies getting out this material; labour suspects it of having a bias on the management side, and management, depending on the agency we are talking about, suspects it of having a labour bias.
Because the centre would be under the control and aegis of labour and management, we would hope such an arrangement would involve a precommitment to accept economic data emanating from this body and in that sense would set realistic parameters within which the collective bargaining could take place. We do not have such ground rules today. We think this will have some measurable impact on the structure of collective bargaining.
We are promoting, in terms of its impact on structures, a greater measure of industry-wide bargaining where it is practical. Part of that objective can be obtained through a legislative approach and, indeed, we are suggesting this in amendments to Part V. Hon. members will note that we talk in terms of allowing the Canada Labour Relations Board to promote coalition of broader-based bargaining in certain circumstances. We will ask the unions and, indeed, encourage them under given circumstances, to form a council of trade unions for collective bargaining purposes.
This proposal has considerable merit from several points of view. To have some impact on the structure of collective bargaining, we have promoted labour education. This does not lend itself to a legislative approach. We have already moved in this direction by way of a grant of $10 million to the Canadian Labour Congress on the basis of $2 million a year, to get under way with an educational program, one which I believe will have very tangible and beneficial results.
I would like to move on now to the third main area of the proposed over-all objectives of this legislation, the initiative to improve the work environment. I think it necessary to address this question so that members can see how the amendments to the Code fit in the over-all context of our desire to achieve perceptible improvements in the work environment. We are the first to admit that these amendments should have an impact on improving the work environment, but pertinent measures to enhance that particular objective do not necessarily lend themselves to a legislative approach. Again, to a large degree they require consultative mechanisms which involve management and labour taking over on an equal basis the operation of some of the institutes that will be required to achieve an improvement in the work environment and a greater degree of humanization in the work place.
December 13, 1977

Many hon. members may recall that about two years ago when we had the Canada Labour Relations Council set up here in Ottawa, labour and management participated on an equal footing with government. The council did considerable work in all these areas analyzing in the Canadian setting the experiments of corporations which had undertaken quality-of-work-life initiatives, various types of industrial democracy, and the impact of these experiments on productivity. These studies were undertaken by management, labour, and government together. 1 think there would have been a noticeable consensus arrived at had not labour felt it had to withdraw from such a body during the controversy over wage and price controls. In any event, we are desirous of setting up a quality of work life centre. We want labour to participate in the operational aspects of this centre, along with management and government. In that sense we do not see this as an offshoot of the bureaucracy but rather as a centre separate from the bureaucracy.
The centre would deal with experiments already taking place in Canada as well as in other countries in the areas of job satisfaction, humanization of the work place and various aspects of industrial democracy. Some of these words are "buzz words" that seem to be having an increasingly controversial impact when discussed in Canada. I will try to avoid getting preoccupied with the controversial nature of the labels and talk about the objectives the quality of work life centre would have. It would seek to guarantee a greater sense of equality in the determination of working conditions and job security, a greater sense of participation by labour with management in the determination of those working conditions and job security.
I would be the first to declare, if there are any comments with reference to this, that we do not see this as repugnant to the collective bargaining system.
In the North American context collective bargaining is the primary instrument in industrial democracy. It will continue to be our primary instrument to ensure that workers have a say in the determination of wages and working conditions. At the same time we note that some countries with a very strong and free labour movement have a better economic performance than ours and in some cases fewer strikes than we do. We note also that in such countries there has been a readiness to complement the collective bargaining system by another system which would ensure co-operation in terms of objectives to be achieved through a non-confrontation route.
As we all know, the collective bargaining system is primarily dependent upon an adversarial approach. We should like to see a complementary system as an overlay on the collective bargaining system. This would provide a means of developing at least a broad consensus in Canada between management and labour within which the collective bargaining system could operate with greater success and greater benefit to workers and management alike.
I might say that some of those countries whose economic performance has been better than our own and which do have a very strong and free labour movement have been prepared to
Canada Labour Code
look at worker-directors on boards, workers' councils at the plant level, and so on. The reaction so far in Canada has been somewhat negative on the part of both labour and management. So we, as a government, are saying, without prejudging the matter: let us have an institute which will look into the whole area and see whether some of those attributes cannot be applied in the Canadian context. They are the provisions which provide for the right to refuse work under conditions which a worker perceives to be dangerous to himself; and the proposals dealing with health and safety committees of workers and management at the plant level.
These provisions would fit nicely into the functions of an institute of occupational health and safety, which again would not be part of the bureaucracy but would be under the aegis of management, labour and government. This would provide the parties, on an ongoing basis, with the latest scientific findings respecting noxious substances which form part of the new technological processes being adopted in the work place to an ever increasing degree. A study of this might possibly involve the necessity of further regulations to protect the health and safety of the worker.
Another area of examination which we think would contribute to an over-all improvement in the work environment is a study of the concept of worker sabbaticals, or paid educational leave. This is part of the 14 points. We would like management and labour to come together with government to study the implications of that particular concept. When advanced in that way, of course, it does not lend itself at this stage to legislative treatment.
If the amendments proposed to the Canada Labour Code under the heading of "justice in the work place" and under the heading of "improvement in procedures and structures of the collective bargaining system" are passed, then we may go a long way to improve the lot of the workers of Canada and, at the same time, improve our industrial relations system.
We have come to the conclusion, as a result of conversations that we have had with many people on the management side and on the labour side, that governments in Canada today, both federal and provincial, the labour movement, and management are operating under more severe constraints than have been the case over the decades. These constraints have been imposed by economic situations throughout the world which do not provide governments with the manoeuvrability or the options which are commonly perceived by many people. Whatever the political complexion of government in Canada, the policies of governments do not differ to any significant degree because the constraints are so severe. I need only mention to my hon. friends in the New Democratic Party that NDP governments have found there was some merit in supporting wage and price controls for a period of time. So constraints are there.
The necessity to be competitive is very much on the mind of many labour leaders, certainly those in the secondary manufacturing field in Canada at the present time.

December 13, 1977
Canada Labour Code
If that is true and there is an increasing realization of it, then it seems to me that exclusive reliance on confrontation, which is so much a part of our collective bargaining system, when it comes to resolving labour disputes and indeed become very passe. Many have come to the conclusion that we must develop another type of system which is complementary to that system.
In other words, attitudes in Canada are changing. I think people are looking with increasing skepticism on some of the old rhetoric. People like my hon. friend, the financial critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), will agree that workers and labour leaders are not calling representatives of the business interests "robber barons" to quite the extent they used to. I also detect that some people on the business side are not quite so ready to go around identifying labour as totally irresponsible in every given situation. There is an increasing sense of community of interest on the part of all.
We do not deny, despite the realization that the old rhetoric has had its day and is archaic thinking, that there is still a great deal to be done in terms of changing fundamental attitudes in Canada. We need this before we can ever get the kind of complementary system that is necessary to soften the total reliance on the adversary approach which is so much part of our system.
By the House adopting these amendments, and to the degree that they enhance our capability of achieving some of the other objectives which I have identified and which do not lend themselves to legislative treatment, we hope to accomplish the change in attitude on the part of labour and management which is so necessary for improving our industrial relations system.
