speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to reply to my hon. friend, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), it would not be amiss-it has certainly been noted by the House-to remark that after a quick flurry over the provisions of the amendments to the Canada Labour Code the minister spent a good deal of his speech commenting on his 14 points and his non-legislative proposals for a better industrial climate for this country. It was not too many months ago that we heard a good deal of this speech, and 1 think I said in good humour-I am sure it was taken in that fashion-that the minister has made the speech so often now that he really does not need any more speech writers.
I say with all sincerity that the minister is desirous of bringing about a better state of industrial relations in this country. Certainly he has made a great many speeches trying to persuade the Canadian public, especially the labour movement, that this is so. The difficulty is that he has been operating under very trying conditions, most of which have been created by the actions of his own cabinet colleagues.
1 should like to come to some of the points which have to be considered when one looks at labour legislation and industrial relations. I suppose that when one tries to find the key to better relations between labour and management, labour and

government, or labour, management, and government together, the first word to start with is "trust". This may not all be the fault of the Minister of Labour. His difficulty over the last several years has been largely that labour in this country no longer trusts the government of the day.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: And the minister knows why.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
The minister knows why. But there is a limit as to how many times the Minister of Labour can make a speech of good intentions against a backdrop of evidence of bad intentions-and not just bad intentions, but thoroughly dishonest changes in government policy and in the word that the government gave to labour.
1 ask all hon. members to remember that in 1974, when this party openly and honestly advocated controls, the government of the day, in a frantic attempt to regain power, denied that it would ever place controls on the working people and the public of this country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: That is what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) said in Hamilton.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: That promise was accepted by labour in Canada right across this country, and because labour in this country believed that the government fighting for re-election meant what it said, in many cases they voted for candidates of that government in the honest belief that they could depend upon ministers of the government when they said there would be no controls.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: They won't be fooled again.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
I cannot guarantee that, because the government is pretty skilful at beguiling the various segments of the Canadian community into believing it, even if that belief, in terms of history, does not last very long.
In an item in a newspaper of November 21 there was an interesting comment in connection with the doublecross to which I am referring. This is an article discussing the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald). This is what the newspaper clipping says:
Someone found some of 'Thumper's' old pamphlets that hadn't been distributed during the 1974 election campaign. They made for funny reading.
'. . . The Tories propose freezing your wages. But even if your wage is frozen, the price of imports cannot be. For example, the prices of simple everyday things like imported oranges may continue to rise, but your wages won't if they're frozen. So you lose.
'The Tories' solution was tried in the United States. It produced shortages of foodstuffs and other supplies and even higher prices when the freeze ended. As a result, the U.S. abandoned it. Britain tried it. It produced confrontation and violence.
'The Tories can't be allowed to freeze your wages. It just won't work. You know it. We know it.'
That is what the election propaganda said. Anybody who says that a qualification was put on that commitment to labour has
December 13, 1977

only to read the propaganda put out in the campaign by one of the former ministers of the cabinet.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: They sit over there laughing at us.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
The author of the article goes on to say what we know and what labour knows. Tie says:
Fifteen months later, Mr. Macdonald introduced wage and price controls.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: Look at how they laugh over there.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
When we talk about a better climate for industrial relations, it is all very well for the minister tonight to talk about it with the backdrop of inflation going down. That is a laugh, after today's figure of 9.1 per cent. It is all very well for the Minister of Labour, working under the cataclysmic chaos that his fellow cabinet members have created, to be tossed out into the maelstrom and told, "You are the Minister of Labour, go and placate these people. Tell them that things are getting better, tell them we'll get them jobs by improving industrial relations". The Minister of Labour has clearly the most difficult task of any member of cabinet when it comes to trying to persuade labour that they should listen to him, no matter how honestly he may be advancing propositions which he sincerely believes are in the interests of the Canadian general public and the labour force.
What happened that has created so much difficulty for the Minister of Labour? Labour walked out of the Canada Labour Relations Council which the minister established and to which he has referred tonight, and which we supported because it was a move in the right direction. What happened to the Economic Council of Canada? Its usefulness and credibility immediately diminished because again labour walked out of it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: Adding to an already unhealthy statistical strike record, labour, in a most unusual step in this country, decided to have what they call a national day of protest, but it was nothing more or less than a national strike. It was not a strike against management in the hundreds, in the thousands of work places of this country. It was a strike against the government and it was a way of saying, "We don't trust these guys, they doublecrossed us and we have got to show them".

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CERTAIN SECTIONS OF THE ACT
speechtext:
Nobody is advocating another such demonstration. It is the antithesis of our system and no members of the House can condone it. But when we talk about having a better climate, a better relationship between government and labour, or management and labour in the work places of this country, in the name of heaven let hon. members remember who has destroyed any hope of creating that climate, at least for a long time to come.
It also had another effect. It had the effect of the Canadian Labour Congress at its meeting in May of 1976 enunciating a manifesto. That manifesto called for a tripartite decision-mak-
Canada Labour Code
ing body of government, management and labour, and because it was decision-making, it was rejected by all political parties. Eventually it was also rejected by some of the affiliates of the Canadian Labour Congress. Months later, in an attempt to salvage the better aspects of the concept, the emphasis shifted to a consultative tripartite arrangement, which was much looser.
Attempts were made by labour and management to have an effective conversation with the government, but what was the government's response? Hon. members should remember that until a few weeks ago, just before the mini-budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was still trying to blackmail the CLC executive into giving a promise of restraint, when he knew, the cabinet knew, the Minister of Labour knew, and everybody with any brains in the country knew that the CLC could not give that commitment because they do not control their affiliates. Yet right until the mini-budget which declared the end of controls, the Prime Minister was trying to blackmail labour into giving a commitment that they could not give.
I do not have to give a lecture on the internal workings of the labour movement to hon. members and I should not have to give it to members of the government. I certainly should not have to give it to the Minister of Labour who knows perfectly well how much difficulty that created in the backrooms and in the organizations of the Canadian Labour Congress. Let me just assure hon. members that on this side we realize that, imperfect as the Canadian Labour Congress may be, it is the single most significant focal point for labour in this country, and if there are to be negotiations, if there is to be a treatment of reason, the CLC cannot be embarrassed and put in a position where it cannot deal with the government. But that is what happened as a result of the Prime Minister's blackmail.
What has happened is that there has been a breakdown of any trust between the labour movement and the government, although, curiously and interestingly enough, there has been more consultation between management and labour in the last year than probably at any time earlier in our history. What does that mean? It means that management recognized that there was no way out of this morass unless they ignored the blandishments of the government or the entreaties of the government and dealt with labour by themselves. That is exactly what has happened.
We remember the next doublecross. As hon. members will remember, the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines clearly indicated that if in the coming year of 1978 inflation did not decrease to 6 per cent or less, there would be provision for allowing wage increases above 6 per cent. That commitment to labour was broken. I say with sincerity that the Minister of Labour knows the effect that had on the climate of accord which he has been attempting to establish.
The minister referred a few minutes ago to the difficulties Canada is facing. It is a comfort to realize that the hon. Minister recognizes them. We would be more comfortable if

we were convinced that other members of the government recognized them. There is no question that most of the observers of the political scene recognize them.
Mr. Bruce Hutchison wrote in an article dated December 12, 1977:
The government can no longer count exclusively, or even primarily, on the issue of the nation's unity when bread and butter issues are over-shadowing it. Hence Mr. Trudeau's belated interest in finance ...
A few weeks ago the Prime Minister delivered a lecture which might have got him through first year economics but not much farther.

Hence Mr. Trudeau's belated interest in finance and Jean Chretien's desperate efforts to control a ruinous inflation, a high unemployment rate and an inherited budgetary deficit that, in normal times, would be enough to sink any government...
The losses are clear to everyone-a mountain of debt, both foreign and domestic, savings eroded, our dollar devalued, our reputation throughout the world gravely damaged.
It is against a background of broken promises and most serious economic difficulties that the minister has the unenviable task of trying to maintain a link between the government of the day and the labour movement. I will give him credit for trying. As everyone is aware, he is operating under difficult circumstances.
The public of Canada should be reminded that federal jurisdiction in labour matters is extremely limited. The minister referred to extra labour propositions. These propositions will have only a limited effect if they are established, because approximately only 10 per cent of the work force in Canada comes within federal jurisdiction. There are approximately ten million people in Canada's labour force and, of that approximately 10 per cent come under the jurisdiction of this House. The rest come under the jurisdictions of the ten provinces and are subject to various provincial labour codes. The workers within federal jurisdiction are subject to the Canada Labour Code. It is important to realize that they include federal servants who are subject to the Public Staff Relations Act.
The 1977 figures indicate that, of the total Canadian work force, 3,149,213 are unionized. The Canadian Labour Congress membership includes 99 unions. Of these, 14 unions have 50,000 members or more. I do not need to list all the unions, but it is important to remember that in the private sector and under federal jurisdiction, and as a consequence subject to the Canada Labour Code, there are approximately 550,000 workers. The most recent figures indicate that approximately 45 per cent of these workers are non-unionized. In addition, approximately 320,000 public servants come within federal jurisdiction and are subject to the Public Service Staff Relations Act. The unionized workers within federal jurisdiction, subject to the Canada Labour Code, are represented by approximately 55 unions, excluding directly chartered CLC and CNTU unions, 40 of which are affiliated with the CLC. The unionized federal public servants are represented by 13 unions, of which eight are affiliated with the CLC.
[Mr. Fraser. 1
A few minutes ago the minister set out the general areas of federal jurisdiction. In summary, the federal jurisdiction involves 550,000 people who are private sector employees and 320,181 people who are public sector employees. If the Armed Forces, the RCMP and others are added to those figures, which is approximately another 100,000 people, the total is just under one million. In the private sector, just over one half are unionized and have the right to strike under the Canada Labour Code, and in the public sector approximately 90 per cent have the right to strike. In the public sector the remaining 10 per cent are senior executives, personnel administrators, the operational methods group, and certain designated essential service employees.
I have taken the time to refer to those statistics because far too often people in the private sector among the public, and within the labour movement, seem to believe that the federal government can effect the answers to a better industrial climate or can solve all the problems that accompany labour and management relations in Canada.
As the minister is aware, the significance of the federal position is the example it sets. As a consequence, any legislation which is passed becomes a signal to the provinces, the labour unions, the private sector from the management side, and the majority of organized and non-organized workers in the rest of the country. It is helpful to enunciate some of the principles which must be kept in mind when one considers legislation in this vital field, and when one is dealing with labour and with management in the hope of establishing better industrial relations.
The first is trust: labour must be able to believe in the government of the day. Without that, all the blandishments and enticements will not work. The second is confidence: both labour and management must believe the government accepts its responsibility to restrain its growth and encroachment on the economy. The degree the government has been increasing its encroachment on the economy has reduced the effectiveness of our private sector to plan, invest, build, and has taken money out of the pockets of the working people. It now ill behooves the government to ask the working people of Canada to bear the brunt of inflation. Of course that has been the complaint of labour, and almost every objective observer in the last two years has indicated that there is much justification in that complaint.
The third is the recognition of the necessity to maintain a free collective bargaining system. The Minister of Labour indicated that is the basis of his own approach, as well as many other things. No matter how helpful some complementary additions to the collective bargaining system may be, I do not believe the country is ready to accept any real, severe encroachment upon the free collective bargaining system. The country is not ready for that yet, and in fact may never be.
In considering legislation and in dealing in an extra legislative manner, as has been suggested by the minister, there is a fundamental point. The fundamental point which has to be remembered is that we have had a history of free collective
December 13, 1977

bargaining, and both management and labour want to get back to it as soon as possible.
The fourth point is that in considering these matters there has to be a minimum of government interference in the terms of collective agreements. By that I am not saying that there has not been in the past-and there may well be in the future; there may be now-occasions when labour must submit to legislative moves in the interests of standards. The minister has spoken about some of these, but in dealing with both management and labour it is essential that it be remembered that both management and labour have chosen to work out most of these problems and arrive at collective agreements over the bargaining table.
The fifth point is that there should be a recognition that foreign structures and foreign philosophies of labour relations cannot be transferred to Canada easily. In fact in some cases they may not be able to be transferred at all.
There has been, especially in recent years-partly because of the very high incidence of strikes in this country, which has, fortunately, diminished very significantly during this past year-an almost frantic yearning to go outside Canada to find some panacea to all our woes, and import it here. The government has even paid some distinguished gentlemen to travel abroad-

As the minister says, one of these gentlemen is from British Columbia, and there is no doubt that in this ongoing debate he has made a significant contribution. 1 had occasion to discuss Mr. Connag-han's report with German trade union people and with members of the German government a year ago, and they complimented Mr. Connaghan on the accuracy with which he portrayed the situation in Germany. However, it is important to recognize also that when one goes to Europe one is constantly warned-as I know the Minister of Labour is aware-that what may work in Germany works because the people there are Germans, and what may work in the Scandinavian countries works there because the people are Scandinavians, but those things may not necessarily work here.
Let me say something about so-called co-determination. It is the view of this party that if both management and labour wish to experiment with forms of co-determination at any level in the work place or in the upper echelons of management, they should be free to do so, but it is also the position of this party that it would be dangerous to force such co-determination by way of legislation. It is far better to achieve these things by voluntary consent in those areas of industry where conditions lend themselves to them than to try to impose them by government edict.
On this same point I noticed that the Minister of Labour did not mention tonight his multi-partite national forum. I am
Canada Labour Code
sure-and I am watching him smile-he did not think I was going to go through my entire speech tonight without mentioning it. I remind the minister and the members of the government that one of the difficulties in achieving this multipartite national forum is that management is not very enthusiastic about it and labour is opposed to it. No matter how good the idea may be in theory, it cannot be brought about unless the parties consent freely to join in such a proposal.
The sixth point is that in developing labour legislation we must be sure to ensure a balance of power in the bargaining process, favouring neither management nor labour, and to the degree that any labour legislation tilts the balance one way or another it works against a climate of accord over the bargaining table.
The seventh point which must be kept in mind-and this is a serious matter which has been avoided by the government for some years-is that at last in this country there must be a realistic acceptance that there are some strikes in essential services, and those strikes which may not start off as essential service strikes but which are demonstrably against the public interest must be dealt with more competently than they are dealt with at the present time. The most recent example was the air traffic controllers' strike, but there have been others: the rail strike of a few years ago, the strike at the river ports on the St. Lawrence, and the grain strike at Halifax. The Minister of Labour has been through all those strikes, and we all tried, given the limitations of present legislation and present approaches, to do the best we could with them.
However, I have to say seriously that despite the fact that this matter was met years ago by the Woods Report, and despite the fact that over and over again the government has finally had to act-usually belatedly-no serious effort has been made by the government to deal with this problem. There is no question that the climate of distrust between the government and labour at the moment probably makes it almost impossible to discuss the matter, but if the government is not discussing it, I can assure the minister that the public is. We have advocated for a long time the establishment of a public interest disputes commission. There are certain aspects of this approach which need consideration, and 1 would be the first to say-and I say it to the minister and to other hon. members, keeping in mind my admonition of a few minutes ago-that these things should not be done without consultation with both labour and management. It is time we started to consider some approaches which are less damaging, not just to the public interest but also to the image of labour, because in the long run it does no good to have problems occurring over and over again which place labour in the unenviable position of having everybody point at it as being the source of all the problems of the country.
I think it is worth considering that a commission-or some other body which has available to it expertise and some of the data the minister spoke about-should monitor at a certain point certain negotiations, and that well before the legal strike date is arrived at, the commission should report to the cabinet on what the effects on the public would be. That report should

Canada Labour Code
be made public because it is essential in dealing in this very delicate area that the public fully understands not only the issues in the dispute but also the effect on the well-being of the country if the dispute cannot be settled.
That report should be made available to the public and to the government, well in advance of the strike date. At that point the cabinet could assess, on the basis of that report, what its responsibility ought to be, and could move in advance of the strike under legislation which could be established to postpone strikes for a certain period of time and to provide for a cooling off period and for a further period of negotiation, with as much help as possible from the commission, from a data centre or from the other bodies the minister has suggested, in order to resolve the dispute without the necessity of putting the country through the agony of a national shutdown. This approach may not always work, but surely it is worth trying. It is a thousand times better than the ad hoc system followed by the government in the years since I came to the House of Commons in 1972. Only subsequent to a cooling off period and further negotiations, if the government felt there was no alternative but to end a strike in a particular area, would legislation to do so be introduced in this House.
The circumstances that surrounded the air controllers' strike must not be repeated. In that case the legislation itself set the terms of the settlement and, as this party has said over and over again, that is completely wrong. This House is not the place to set the terms of settlement. It was doubly wrong in that case because it was the employer-this House-that passed the legislation setting the terms of settlement. If settlement is to be forced on both sides the matter must be taken out of this House and put before an independent arbitrator.
Another matter that must be faced because of growing concern in the country is democracy in the unions themselves. I say that, realizing that there is democracy in the vast majority of unions. But where there is seen to be a limitation of democracy and something less than a free and secret vote, the public's confidence in the union movement is diminished. We have instances such as happened only today when allegations were made in this House with respect to the illegal strike in the postal service. Illegal strikes within federal jurisdiction-within the public service-cannot be allowed to take place with impunity. I say that because the working people of this country have to realize, as I think most do, that their freedom and security can only be maintained under the rule of law. To the degree that some union leaders are prepared to take members out on illegal strikes, they will destroy the faith and confidence of the general public in the trade union movement.
Another point is that the law and the process of union organization-application for certification and creation of a first contract-must not be unfairly hindered. I say that because, looking back in history, we must recognize that unions were necessary and, I believe, are still necessary. I think it is also accurate to say that the existence of trade unions and

of a union movement is accepted by the vast majority of Canadians as part of our industrial milieu.
Another aspect is that the Canada Labour Relations Board has to be made more efficient. Union after union and management after management complain of delays and I am sure the minister has heard these complaints. I urge him to consider steps to make that board more efficient in the sense of being able to move the disputes more quickly because, to the degree that they are held up, they aggravate the situation.

I recognize that, but I would also ask the minister to recognize, as I am sure he does, that much more must be done.
I also want to emphasize that labour legislation must concern itself with its effect on productivity. That does not mean just a one-way street. It is essential for management to have a productive work force, but it is also essential for management to remember that decent conditions and high morale lead to a much more efficient and productive work force.
My last point, Mr. Speaker, is to say that the answer to industrial relations is not-I repeat not-just to pass more laws. Canada has a vexingly legalistic system now. There are ten provincial codes and a federal code. Every month of the year high salaried people try to figure out how to bring them all in line. Passing another law is no solution. It must be remembered also that the system is, and in a free society always will be, an adversary system to a certain degree. There are differences of position and differences of interest, but when passing legislation the object of the exercise is to increase the level of understanding of each side for the other in the adversary process. In a free society both sides should be grown up enough to be able to handle freedom, and should have enough common sense to know when to dump rhetoric and face the facts. If management or labour wants the government to settle everything, believe me, government is all too ready to move in. It is easy to force a settlement, but it is often difficult for either side to live with it.
We believe there are no magic answers to industrial relations in Canada. What we are talking about are human relations, and anyone-labour leader, public spokesman or politician-who offers an instant answer or an omniscient remedy for the frailties of human nature is selling the public a pig in a poke.
I see my time is getting short, Mr. Speaker, but I beg your indulgence and the indulgence of the House to carry on.

This bill is not entirely accepted by either management or labour. For instance the effect of the higher legislated standards has to be carefully considered. The danger is, of course, that legislated standards intrude on the collective bargaining system, as both management and labour have remarked.
As I mentioned a few minutes ago, the Canada Labour Relations Board is faced with the accusation that it cannot handle its present workload, and to the extent that the bill increases work for members of the board it must be made certain that these amendments are appropriate and that the board can handle the extra work.
Some areas where work will be increased by the broadening of the board's discretionary powers are the following: altering terms of employment; imposition of first agreements; onus of proof; cease and desist orders; consent to prosecute; remedies for unfair practices; compliance with board orders; representation and run-off votes and others. That is not to say there are problems that cannot be surmounted; it is to say it is going to require careful consideration of the proposals which the minister has put forward.
It would be appropriate for a committee to ask the minister whether consideration has been given to the cost of these amendments and whether that cost will be reflected in price increases or operators' costs, especially in small business. When I mention small businesses there is an interesting comment made by Mr. John Bulloch, head of the Independent Business Association of Canada, in a speech which he delivered November 21 at Queen's University. He said this:
The small business sector is the most free enterprise oriented part of our entire economy and, as such, finds it difficult-if not impossible-to flourish in an atmosphere which rewards non-productivity. The magnitude of this problem is best appreciated in the light of one basic statistic: The small business sector is responsible for about half of the jobs provided by the entire private sector.
That has to be kept in mind, Mr. Speaker. It also has to be taken into account that labour is suspicious of legislation that moves into the unorganized area because it will then take away from labour its legitimate area of activity.
Mr. Speaker, labour is going to ask us to consider carefully the averaging provisions which it feels establish too much discretion, specifically that there is too much discretionary power in the hands of the minister in the amendments to section 29 which allows the permit to be issued and cancelled at the employers' request. Mr. Speaker, in this bill the minister proposes a number of improvements in the situation of Canadian citizens who come under federal jurisdiction. We should keep in mind, of course, that only about 10 per cent of the labour force in Canada comes under the jurisdiction of the federal government, and that 90 per cent of the working people in this country fall under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. None of the improvements proposed here will immediately, or in the near future, improve the lot of Canadians who come under provincial jurisdiction.
We welcome the improvements which will benefit Canadians who come under federal jurisdiction-the removal of pregnancy as a cause for dismissal, the requirement that employers pay salaries on a regular basis, the extra day holiday-Boxing Day-the proposals to give workers some rights with respect to health and safety. However, I must say to the minister that I have a great deal of suspicion that most of these will remain simply as clauses on statute books, and very few of them will become effective. I will deal with that in greater detail a little later.
The minister will not be surprised at our support of these proposals; in fact they are long overdue. And he should not be surprised if his proposals have been met with less than 100 per cent enthusiasm by the spokesmen for organized labour in this country. They recognize the fact that these improvements are very minor as compared to the tremendous damage which has been done to the Canadian people by the fact that we have the greatest percentage of unemployed that this country has had since before World War II.
Some members of parliament, myself included, are old enough to remember the hungry, dirty thirties. We have now, Mr. Speaker, more unemployed, and as large a percentage of our labour force as there was unemployed-not in 1933-but

during the period 1937 to 1939. The unemployment was only eliminated by the advent of World War II when we suddenly found that we could do all the things government said could not be done during that great depression. We found we had the money to put people to work building guns, tanks and planes, all of which were destroyed during the war, even though during the earlier years we could not put them to work building the things which needed so much to be built.
That situation is with us again. Last month on a seasonally adjusted basis we had 900,000 unemployed, 8.4 per cent of the labour force, a id among our young people almost twice that percentage unemployed.
In Manitoba, which never has the highest percentage of people employed or the highest unemployed, last month it had 28,000 unemployed, an increase in the rate of unemployment from 4.7 per cent in October to 6.1 per cent in November.
Given this tremendous calamity, it is not surprising that organized labour, which to a large extent holds this government responsible for our high unemployment, is not enthused by these proposals. The labour movement is suspicious of this government. No matter how attractive government legislation or proposals may be, the labour movement is not prepared to listen to them. One cannot blame it.
Let us look briefly at what has happened in the last two years under a government which was elected to a large extent by telling the Canadian people that it was opposed to, and would not impose, wage and price controls. Despite that promise, a year later it brought them in under the so-called anti-inflation program.
We in the New Democratic Party opposed that program. We said it would not work. The government brought in that program in 1975 because it said inflation was rampant. There was double digit inflation. The inflationary rate on an annual basis was 10'/2 per cent. The government said it had to deal with that, and put limits on wage and price increases.
There was a temporary reduction in the increase in the cost of living. According to figures that came out yesterday, the cost of living in the past 12 months increased by 9.1 per cent. Given an increase between 3/10 and 7/10 of a percentage point each month, as we have had for the past 11 months, when we get the figures for December we will find that for the calendar year 1977 the increase in the cost of living has been about 9Vi per cent, just 1 per cent less than when the government implemented its anti-inflation program.
We opposed the anti-inflation program because it would not be equitable. We pointed out that it would be easy to control wages and salaries, but difficult if not impossible to control increases for self-employed people and professionals. Time has shown that we were correct. In fact increases in income of professionals such as doctors, lawyers, dentists, engineers and architects have been substantially higher than those permitted to wage and salary workers.
[Mr. Orlikow.l
The last decision of the government, a complete repudiation of its arguments when it brought in its anti-inflation program, was to limit increases in wages and salaries in 1978 to 6 per cent. It is obvious to everyone but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) that the cost of living in 1978 will undoubtedly increase by somewhere between 8 and 10 per cent.
By bringing in legislation to limit wage and salary increases to 6 per cent, the government is decreeing that the majority of the Canadian people will have a real reduction in their living standard in 1978. When it brought in the anti-inflation program, it was ostensibly because wage and salary increases were running substantially higher than the increase in the cost of living. We have had a betrayal of the interests of the ordinary people of this country by the government. Therefore it is not surprising that the labour movement is lukewarm about this or any other proposal by the government.
I want to say something else about the economic situation before dealing with some of the basic principles of the bill.
As bad as the government's anti-inflation program has been in terms of creating more unemployment, its policy of restraint, supported by the Conservative party, is an even greater disaster for the country in terms of creating more employment.
There are only two fields in which people can find employment in this country. One is the private sector. That sector employs people only when it can produce and sell its products at a profit. When the economy is in recession, as is the economy of Canada and the economies of most of the industrialized world, the private sector does not hire more people. It lays them off. We have seen a host of layoffs of long term employees in recent weeks and months. I could spend my 40 minutes just listing those companies, beginning with International Nickel, Falconbridge, Noranda, and Northern Telecom.
The other field in which people find work is with the government or on projects initiated by the government such as housing, schools, hospitals and so on. At this time, when the private sector is laying off people, federal, provincial and municipal governments should be hiring more people. Instead of putting more people to work, the Liberal government and the official opposition join in a call for more restraint. More restraint will mean more unemployment. In the coming year the rate of unemployment will not be the present 8 per cent plus, but probably 9 per cent. In fact I will not be surprised if it is above 9 per cent in 1978. In fact given this situation, one can understand why labour is suspicious about this bill.
I wish the minister well in the appeals he has made and will continue to make with regard to the need for better co-operation between labour, management, and government with regard to more consultation, working on forms of industrial democracy, and so on. However, they are just words. I do not blame the minister for making those speeches. However, they are much like the sermons that many ministers preach on Sunday mornings, having tittle relevance to life as it is in Canada. The same is true with regard to the view that is frequently expressed that we should try to emulate the peace
December 13, 1977

which exists between labour and management in countries such as Sweden and Germany. That peace is based on entirely different conditions than we have or have had in Canada. That peace is based on full employment.
It is relatively easy to get workers and their unions to be successful and co-operative and objective when they have jobs and when they have reason to believe those jobs will continue. It is another thing to persuade workers to be co-operative and reasonable when they do not know whether they will be working or not in a week's time or a month's time. We should not be surprised if, in such circumstances, they try to squeeze out every benefit they can right then.
Then again, it is recognized in a great many countries that unions are here to stay, that they are part of the way in which society operates. Unfortunately this is not always the case in Canada. Many employers, particularly employers in small business, and some in business which is not so small, do everything they can to discourage their employees from joining unions. I have no doubt that the banks, for example, are, and will be, less than enthusiastic about workers wishing to show an interest in joining trade unions. So it is not surprising that workers and trade unions are edgy about any proposals which come from outside-from management, the media, or even from governments which they believe are somewhat sympathetic to their objectives.
Having already indicated that we support and welcome this bill as far as it is likely to benefit the people who come under the jurisdiction of federal labour legislation, I want to turn to consider some of its provisions. I must say I have a good many reservations about a number of the proposals before us, not with regard to their intention so much as the ability of the department and the government, given their present staffing, to do the things which are outlined in the bill.
For example, this legislation will provide where possible a mechanism by which a non-union worker may complain about his dismissal; he will be able to complain to an inspector of the Department of Labour, and if the inspector cannot settle the point he may request that his complaint be referred to an adjudicator appointed by the minister, and that adjudicator would have the power to order reinstatement and compensation if he finds the employee has been wrongly dismissed. I might point out that workers in Canada have so far not had much success in enforcing a provision along these lines, not even the much milder provision presently in the federal Labour Code. All the experience in Canada and the United States shows that many employers who are opposed to the unionization of their workers will use any and all methods open to them to prevent their workers joining unions. There is no evidence, and I say this with regret rather than with condemnation, that the Department of Labour as presently constituted has the ability to police and enforce a provision of that kind.
The bill contains a clause which gives employees the right to refuse to work if they feel that working conditions constitute imminent danger to their health and safety. The procedure is
Canada Labour Code
that the employee reports such circumstances to his employer who then investigates the problem. If the matter cannot be resolved, a safety officer is called in to make an inspection. Should the employee remain unsatisfied there is provision for an appeal to the Labour Relations Board. Mr. Speaker, the spokesman for the official opposition has already drawn attention to the backlog of work which faces the Labour Relations Board. That is not the only difficulty.
In this period of mass unemployment any worker, particularly in an unorganized plant, who considers making the complaint has to bear in mind the possible effect on his continued employment. To rectify the circumstances about which he has complained might well involve the installation of a costly improvement; a worker is likely to be extremely hesitant about making a complaint because of the possibility of his dismissal.
Another point is this: who decides what the word "imminent" means? What one person may consider to be an imminent danger another might regard as being a necessary or inherent part of the work being done. We shall certainly want to discuss with the minister and his officials in committee precisely how this clause will operate.
Then there is provision for the establishment of health and safety committees in the work place. Such committees would be required in various work places at the discretion of the minister. We approach this provision with a good deal of skepticism. I do not worry too much about the approach taken by the present minister. On the whole I believe that were he to err he would do so on the right side. But we have seen other ministers of labour in whom we would be far less confident.
Employees are to compose 50 per cent of the individual committees whose task would be to identify potential health and safety hazards and to develop management programs related to health and safety. Mr. Speaker, we believe these committees should be set up in all work places employing more than ten people. We do not like the fact that the choice of the members of the committees is left to regulation by the minister. We believe that the employees' representatives, where there is a union, should be chosen by the union, and that when no union exists an election should be held among all the employees. I am doubtful whether the committees could really work in places where there is no union. I suspect employers would put pressure on individual members of the committee who would be inclined to keep in mind at all times the likelihood of their being fired if they made what the employer thought was trouble.
We believe that if and when these committees are set up they must be given training on a regular basis in health and safety aspects at their place of work, that is, if the committees are to function effectively. A committee must decide where and when to hold its meetings, rather than this being left to regulations published under the bill. Committees should also meet at regular intervals.

I want to deal with one more broad question, and this is where I believe the bill is not much more than window dressing. According to the minister, this bill will bring some order and reason into the whole question of occupational health and safety in those places where federal jurisdiction exists over industry. It is pretty obvious that the federal government up until now has been derelict in its duty to protect the health and safety of workers. Because of this neglect, the number of accidents in work places has been increasing at a steady and alarming rate. In 1968 there were 6.5 million accidents. In 1974 the number had almost doubled; there were 11.5 million accidents. These figures relate to all work places, which would include those under federal and provincial jurisdiction; I do not have a more detailed breakdown between those two jurisdictions.
As a result of the increase in the number of accidents there has, of course, been a corresponding increase in the cost of accidents to industry. In 1968 it was estimated that the cost of accidents to industry was $1,165 billion. By 1973 this had increased to $2.1 billion. When this cost is adjusted for increases in consumer prices, there has been a 30 per cent increase in cost over the five year period 1968 to 1973.
The number of days lost through accidents is greater than the number of days lost through strikes and lockouts. We read a great deal about the harm done to our country and to our economy by strikes, but we read and hear very little about the cost to the country of accidents. The number of days lost in 1974 as a result of strikes and lockouts was nine million; the number of days lost through accidents in 1974 was 11.5 million. So one can see that governments, both federal and provincial, have not really addressed themselves to this problem.
The intervention of governments in this area has, to say the least, been ad hoc. There are at least nine federal departments involved in the area, and among them they administer about 10 separate pieces of legislation, all of which are safety oriented and have little regard for health aspects. Even the safety record shows flaws. The Canada Labour Code, which is the major piece of legislation on this subject, covers employees working in federal industry, except those in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and those people who work in shipyards, on trains and planes. These people are covered by separate pieces of legislation, and this legislation will not be improved by the changes proposed in this bill.
We believe that the government should consolidate all occupational health and safety considerations into one department. We believe they should give a great deal more consideration to the health aspects of the work place. We believe they should adopt the philosophy that people in the work place have a right to the same protection as people in the community.
I want to close by pointing out what I consider to be the inability of the minister to communicate with his fellow ministers. The Minister of Labour preaches, I believe sincerely, the need to make great improvements in the way we monitor and control the health and welfare of those who work in business and in industry in this country, while just a few days ago his

colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), said that one of the big reasons for the lay-offs in Sudbury was that pollution controls instituted in that city by the provincial government of Ontario were so tough that industry simply could not afford to live with them. One has only to drive through or fly over Sudbury to get a picture of what the moon looks like, Mr. Speaker, so much of the environment in Sudbury has been destroyed by the fumes and pollutants which have been spewed into the air and into the water over an area covering 50 to 100 square miles. Compare the view of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with the very fine sentiments expressed by the Minister of Labour.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to the extent that there are very specific improvements proposed in this bill, we greet them with approval. But we look on the rest as mostly verbiage, as a plank in the next election platform of the Liberal party, a measure which might be implemented, like other pledges in the past, 25 to 30 years from now. To that extent we are, to say the least, pretty critical of the whole package.

subtopic: FINANCE-REQUEST FOR MEETING BETWEEN GATT NEGOTIATORS AND CERTAIN INDUSTRIES
FINANCE-REQUEST FOR MEETING BETWEEN GATT NEGOTIATORS AND CERTAIN INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though my question was primarily related to agriculture, it was initially directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) since the Minister of Finance introduced the legislation adjusting duties, particularly relating to imports arriving in Canada. Unfortunately, seven minutes does not give one anything like enough time to do more than raise questions, so I want to ask a series of questions this evening.
Has the minister compared the relative trade opportunities Canadian agriculture has when shipping to the U.S. versus the opportunities United States agriculture has when shipping to Canada? Has he examined the opportunities for Canadian agriculture to ship to the European Economic Community compared with their opportunities to ship to the Canadian market? Has he examined the opportunities of the most favoured nations to ship to us compared with our opportunity to ship to them? Has the minister ever taken these matters into consideration?
December 13, 1977

Has the minister assessed the impact of the formation of the EEC, particularly as it relates to apples and to Canadian trade in the European market, and to other commodities as well? Has he examined the relative position to date versus the relative position of 20 years ago? Has the minister examined the graphs to show the pattern of Canadian agricultural trade as it relates primarily to fruits and vegetables in the last twenty years? Does he know how much the imports, for instance, of apples have increased, and is he familiar with the decrease in the apple exports from Canada? If he does not have the answers to these questions, then he is in no way competent to pass legislation or, as Minister of Finance, to be a party to the decision as to what trading considerations shall be extended to other nations entering our market.
Does the minister fully understand the impact of the recommendations of the Tariff Board as they have broadened the NOP category to include a number of products not clearly defined, and does he know that as this NOP group is expanded at lower rates of duty, these imports will infringe upon markets for Canadian producers? If he does not, then Canada is not in very good hands when legislation is introduced or when our negotiators go abroad.
Does the minister know that the production of Canadian fruits and vegetables on a larger scale with a better degree of protection, might very well provide the consumers with better prices than they are presently getting from a starved Canadian horticultural industry, plus imports from other lands? Has the minister studied the impact upon our costs of the lowering of duty structures on such items as tomatoes and tomato products, because if he did, he would understand that the cost of tomato products coming into Canada today exceeds what Canadian agriculture would need to produce Canada's requirements in a normal year.
Does the minister know that if all of the recommendations of the Canadian Horticultural Council to the Tariff Board hearings would cost Canadian consumers 33 cents per capita a year, the increase in tax returns to the Canadian government would far exceed 33 cents per capita a year? Does he know that, according to the federal Bureau of Statistics' figures, it is estimated by the Canadian food processing industry that if their recommendations were accepted for the importation of processed products, it would cost Canadians 48 cents per capita a year? We are talking peanuts in respect of protection for the consumer when we are talking about 48 cents per capita a year, but we are talkimg about the expansion of a multi-million-dollar industry and the employment that would go with it.
Does the minister know that when the United States is preparing its case for negotiations, the industry is part of the preparation and a party to the negotiations and that they are guided by the industry? Is the minister prepared to allow comparable input and comparable work along with that group, or is he not? Has the minister checked what has been given away in the last twenty years as we have negotiated tariffs,
Adjournment Debate
and what we have received? Have we been Santa Claus or have we been Scrooge?
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) summed that up when he said that when agriculture goes to Geneva, it goes in a bikini, indicating it has very little more to give.
Will the minister insist that the Canadian negotiating team get the surtax which has been requested by both the processing industry and the fresh fruit and vegetable industry, with a triggering device that will be activated in time to preserve the Canadian agricultural industry, or will he allow it to continue on the basis of the dumping legislation which cannot be an effective mechanism for the protection of the industry? Does the minister know-I will cite the extreme of change in trade-that in the last ten years mushroom imports and mushroom products have increased by 1,600 per cent? Does he know that mushroom imports today now constitute 70 per cent of the Canadian market?
Since my time is about up, I want to ask the minister for an answer to my initial question: is he prepared, and is the government prepared to support him, in the formation of a house committee to allow the industry and members of the House to present to cabinet ministers and to negotiators, if possible before they go to Geneva, the facts and figures and the needs of the Canadian horticultural and food processing industries of Canada?

The Canadian Trade and Tariffs Committee was established specifically for this purpose. There have also been numerous briefings and discussions between representatives of the private sector, senior government officials and members of the Canadian negotiating, team, and direct consultations with provincial governments, including a federal-provincial ministerial conference in October.
Some members of the opposition have been briefed on the negotiations and have called on the Canadian delegation in Geneva. The office of the co-ordinator for the multilateral trade negotiations has also been very active in publicizing the negotiations in recent months. This office was established to undertake liaison with provincial governments and private sector organizations on the evolution of government policy on the negotiations, and to consult with them on specific issues as they develop during the course of the negotiations.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-VETERINARY COLLEGE FOR ATLANTIC REGION-INQUIRY AS TO COMMITMENT TO FINANCE-REFERENCE OF HOWELL REPORT TO COMMITTEE
AGRICULTURE-VETERINARY COLLEGE FOR ATLANTIC REGION-INQUIRY AS TO COMMITMENT TO FINANCE-REFERENCE OF HOWELL REPORT TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure who will reply to the question I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) earlier regarding the need for a veterinary college in Atlantic Canada. My question results from the report tabled by Dean Howell, who was appointed by the Government of Canada to explore the necessity for a further veterinary college in Canada. There are three such colleges in Canada today. The conclusion of that report was that a fourth college should be established in Atlantic Canada. At the end of the report it was recommended that the college be established in Prince Edward Island.
There are many things I could say about the conclusion reached by this report, but my time is limited during adjournment debate. The fact of the matter is that there are obvious conflicting provincial interests as to where a veterinary college should be established in Atlantic Canada. I have asked the Minister of Agriculture if he would exercise his good office in an attempt to remove the question of where the college should be located from the cross currents of provincial jurisdiction and on to the federal table.
The move to establish another college was commenced long before 1970, but during that year the federal Department of Agriculture undertook a study in order to discover if there was a need, and the department found out there was. Frankly the criteria established by Dean Howell are in open conflict with some of his conclusions. Obviously I am biased concerning the location of the college. It could be and certainly should be in Nova Scotia.
Why should a dean from the Guelph Veterinary College, through his imagination and discussions with Atlantic Canadians, decide to establish a veterinary college in Prince Edward Island? It does not take a professor from Guelph to know that besides lobsters, Prince Edward Island produces potatoes. Prince Edward Island is a field and crop community. I am not knocking P.E.I. because I am a member from the Atlantic community, but the animals in Atlantic Canada are in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There are relatively few in P.E.I., and the criterion established by Dean Howell himself is the need to have a veterinary college established next to a degree-conferring university. At the moment the only university in Prince Edward Island, UPEI, is not a degree-conferring university. We need postgraduate facilities in some of the establishments that are already in Atlantic Canada, not in Prince Edward Island.
In the closing moments of this debate I cannot speak on the need for a veterinary college without going back in history. In the time I have left I hope hon. members will put up with a little nostalgia. This is December 13, 1977. It just so happens that a man called George Nowlan, my father, was elected to this House on December 13, 1948, 29 years ago. Perhaps that was before some hon. members were even born. It was certainly before most of my staff were born. I do not want to get too nostalgic, but it is interesting to look at the Journals of this House. I do not think they have been referred to before in adjournment debates, but as I say, my father was introduced to the House of Commons on January 26, 1949.
Perhaps it is because of the conviviality and informality of the adjournment debate that I trespass this far, but having the opportunity to speak in this Chamber on December 13, I feel I should do no less than to pay some respect to my heritage.
I want to refer to other hon. members who are great Canadians or were great Canadians. The day my father was introduced to this House, Lester Pearson, Albert Boucher, Stuart Garson, Leopold Demers, and a man called George Drew were also introduced. I know that does not solve the problem with regard to a veterinary college in Atlantic Canada, and I am the first to admit that.
Regardless of all the facts I could recite from the lengthy document I have in my hand, the fact of the matter is that we have a research station at Kentville, Nova Scotia, which is one of the most viable research stations under the Department of Agriculture. Any veterinary college should be established next to a research station or near animals. That would certainly be in Nova Scotia, in the Annapolis Valley. Many times I heard my father say that a complementary development next to the research station in Nova Scotia would be a veterinary college. Frankly, that is where the field animals are. Because of what my father said I took unto myself the licence to introduce a little personal nostalgia to this adjournment debate. That is fairly unusual, but any member who has been in this House for a while should be exposed to a little nostalgia from time to time.
The Department of Agriculture has lead the movement to canvass whether there should be a veterinary college. The commissioner appointed by the department says there should be one. I suggest that the minister use his good offices toward this end, but initially we should refer the Dean Howell report to the Standing Committee on Agriculture so that all interested parties can come before it.
If the minister thinks there are other avenues we should explore in order to avoid a provincial fight, I would be happy to go along with him as long as there is progress and as long as a veterinary college is established. We do not need provincial cross-currents and jealousies to stymie what Dean Howell himself says is very necessary.

subtopic: CANADA COUNCIL-PROPOSAL THAT COMMITTEE REVIEW MANDATE
CANADA COUNCIL-PROPOSAL THAT COMMITTEE REVIEW MANDATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I last raised the question of the Canada Council grants and contributions, and the Council's abuse of its privilege to distribute tax dollars for the purpose of elevating the artistic standards of Canada, I have spoken to many reporters, heard from many Canadians, and discussed the matter in several different forums. The almost unanimous response of those who have seen the obscene documentation is outright outrage.
I should like to present this material to the House tonight but I would urge the television cameras not to zoom too close to it because I think it would be offensive to the record as well as to the Canadian people to see it. At this point, although I should like to expose the material to the people of Canada and shock them further, that is not my purpose tonight. The reason for the disgust and anger for the inadequacy of judgment and administrative capacity of the Council and the government goes much deeper than a mere scandalous wastage of hard-earned tax dollars.
This material, supported and masquerading in the name of art, is a demeaning degradation of human experience. It is in my view neither creative nor beautiful, it is not even grotesque or or ugly beautiful, it is neither uplifting nor fulfilling, it is not even passionate or erotic; it is simply vulgar degradation of the human experience-vulgar and demeaning at a level well below that of funky graffiti written on the back of washroom doors. This type of vulgarity deserves to be placed in a category of the hate literature of pop art and should not be censored but rather branded as unfit for human consumption, and discarded on the rubbish heap to rot in its own vulgarity.
This material is evil in the broadest sense of the word, and the government has an obligation to fight against this type of
Adjournment Debate
degradation rather than condoning, supporting, and encouraging the production and distribution of it. This material is not art. It is not right. It is wrong.
The minister, the government, and its vehicle the Canada Council, are weak and full of fear-fearful of not appearing avant garde, fearful of being labelled culturally illiterate. I say that the granting of thousands of dollars for this material proves they do not in fact have the capacity to judge the bottom line of tolerance of either the will of this parliament or the will of the Canadian people.
Not only is the Canada Council supporting literature which most in this House would term obscene, but the Auditor General has lashed out at that body for lack of adequate documentation. Right now it is entirely possible for someone to give the skimpiest budget details, obtain a grant, and spend the first installment in any manner he wishes.
What the Auditor General was more wary of was the unknown abuse of the existing system. In the small sample of grants he examined, requests for documentation of expenses were not complied with. The money could have been spent anywhere and anyhow for all the Canada Council knows.
When I asked in committee whether or not the Canada Council would comply with the Treasury Board regulations calling for tightening up I was informed that they would not do so. That kind of answer does not make the taxpayer-the person who has to put up all this $403 million the Canada Council has spent to date-feel very confident. He likes to know his money is being spent efficiently and effectively, the Canada Council should not be considered a special case for financial accountability on tax dollars.
I have requested that the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts examine the Canada Council's mandate and issue a report of their findings. The body has been with us for 20 years; a time which has been the stage for many changes, and it is time to look at it again.
A parliamentary committee should determine: (1) the nature of the mechanism that will assure accountability to parliament including concerns regarding political direction, financial documentation, and selection criteria; (2) the nature of ministerial responsibility for both financial documentation, grant and contribution selection criteria; (3) a selection process that will ensure that political bias and patronage are not simply replaced with artistic elitist bias and patronage; (4) a selection process that will reflect regional aspirations and realities of our country.
The current minister has directed the Canada Council to begin a program to promote national unity in contradiction of the minister's earlier view that neither the minister nor this

December 13, 1977
Adjournment Debate
parliament should direct Canada Council. While promoting Canada's unity is a worthwhile endeavour, this is an extension of the purpose of objectives of the Council and should on this basis alone be referred to the committee and further legislation, should political direction of the Canada Council be considered acceptable by this parliament. Personally, I view the potential for abuse with alarm because of the implication amply demonstrated within dictatorships, communist or otherwise, who have subverted the arts for political ends.
In September the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) transgressed his oft stated policy that the Canada Council was solely an arms' length organization when he gave $4 million to that body earmarked for national unity projects. The Secretary of State has started an inquiry into the arts; an inquiry outside parliament and the by-passing of parliament is an all too common action during the last few years and parliament demands that right back. Obviously the Secretary of State believes an examination of the Canada Council and its mandate is necessary. Let us turn the issue over to those who represent the people.
In view of the minister's direction to the Canada Council to begin a program to promote national unity in contradiction of the minister's view that neither the minister nor parliament should direct the Canada Council, and in view of the Auditor General's concern regarding financial documentation, I ask the minister to consider requesting that the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts complete a review of the mandate, and the implications of extending that mandate to include promotion of national unity as well as the accountability, financial procedures, and performance to date of the Canada Council.

speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.
Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary
of State): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) essentially raises two questions, the first one being parliament's intention when it established the Canada Council, and second the Canada Council's performance of the task set forth for it by parliament.
As the hon. member is aware, the Canada Council was established in 1957 to foster and promote the study and enjoyment of and production in the arts, humanities and social sciences. Parliamentarians at that time were most concerned that they should guarantee the independence of the Council to ensure its freedom from possible political interference. Indeed the hon. member tonight has high-lighted that particular concern which I suspect indicates that parliament, even today, is concerned and that those concerns remain valid.
The essentials, Mr. Speaker, and some of the history that should be brought forward are that the estimates and the
supplementary estimates for the Canada Council must be reviewed by the appropriate Minister, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts). The Secretary of State must bring the supplementary estimates before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts for approval annually. Indeed, parliament has the opportunity at that time to assess whether the estimates are valid and should go forward.
This brings me to the second question raised by the hon. member, that of the Canada Council's performance. Hon. members, both in committee and in the House, have questioned the Council's emphasis on "excellence", yet I am sure that all those interested in the Council are familiar with its explorations program, designed to seek out new forms of expression and public participation in the arts. In its quest for innovation and the imaginative, the council, through explorations, encourages any Canadian to submit ideas for funding, any Canadian with an imaginative idea and the ability to carry it out.
Unfortunately the member opposite does not afford me the courtesy of an opportunity to express myself as was given to him. I would like to go on at great length to discuss his personal views, but I would like to get to the question he raised and give him the answer he seeks. If he wishes to discuss back and forth and not have the answer given, I am willing to give up that time.
The Canada Council has never spurned the off-beat for fear of public criticism-for excellence wears many guises. The hon. member, in calling for a review of the Council's performance, has referred to "disgusting and pornographic" works by a Canadian poet supported by the Council. I agree that not all works created by contemporary artists-whether or not they are supported by the Canada Council-may find favour with the general public or its elected representatives. However, might I remind the hon. member, that many of those whose names rank among the great painters, poets, and novelists did not enjoy public acclaim in their own lifetimes? Indeed, many were obliged to pursue their art in the face of diversity. And while I am not arguing that the poets mentioned in the hon. member's question to my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), may necessarily prove to be held in great esteem by all posterity, I should like to argue that, unless all forms of expression are encouraged, we can expect of the future no more than a form of limited cultural development which will be in direct proportion to the restraint applied during the critical growth period.
Might I also suggest that the hon. member has selected for his own purposes examples which do not reflect the general
December 13. 1977

activity of the Canada Council and the artists it supports. He is glossing over all those artistic achievements whose success can be attributed to the support received from the Canada Council which is, should, and must be, free from political intercession. I see my time has expired, Mr. Speaker.
